meta.title: Alarum Technologies (ALAR): CEO Shachar Daniel Navigates a Three-Phase Reinvention — From Israeli Cybersecurity Startup to Nasdaq-Listed Web Data Infrastructure Provider, Betting Proxy Networks and AI-Ready Datasets Will Define the Next Decade of Enterprise Intelligence
meta.abstract:
Alarum Technologies Ltd. (Nasdaq/TASE: ALAR) is a Tel Aviv-headquartered web data collection company whose present form is the product of three successive reinventions under co-founder and chief executive Shachar Daniel. The company began life in 2013 as Safe-T Group, a zero-trust network-access and cybersecurity vendor targeting Israeli enterprises. A 2019 inflection point arrived when Safe-T acquired NetNut Ltd. from DiViNetworks Ltd. for $9.7 million, implanting a residential IP proxy network technology that would ultimately consume the parent. Over the following three years the cybersecurity heritage was systematically shed: enterprise security contracts were divested, a consumer privacy-VPN segment was wound down, and NetNut's IP Proxy Network (IPPN) platform emerged as the sole revenue engine. In January 2023, the company formalised the transformation by rebranding to Alarum Technologies Ltd. and migrating its Nasdaq ticker to ALAR.

Today Alarum operates a hybrid proxy network of approximately 85 million IP addresses across datacenter, residential, mobile, and ISP node types, sold under the NetNut brand to enterprise customers conducting large-scale public-web data collection. The product suite spans rotating and static residential proxies, datacenter proxies, a SERP API, a Website Unblocker, and — launched in late 2024 — an AI Data Collector product line designed to serve the surging demand from large language model developers and AI training data pipelines. AI-oriented products accounted for roughly 30 percent of revenues in early 2025, up from four percent in the prior comparable period.

The financial trajectory is instructive. Full-year 2024 revenues reached $31.8 million, up 20 percent year-over-year, with web data collection specifically growing 45 percent to $30.9 million. The company turned net-profitable in 2024 ($5.8 million net profit versus a $5.6 million loss in 2023) and generated $8.9 million in operating cash flow. Cash and liquid investments stood at $25.0 million at year-end 2024, providing a balance-sheet cushion unusual for a micro-cap SaaS operator. Yet the first quarter of 2025 showed a revenue step-down to $7.1 million (minus 15 percent year-over-year), attributed to demand headwinds from certain customer cohorts and deliberate reinvestment in next-generation infrastructure, raising questions about whether the 2024 growth rate can be restored. This dossier examines the strategic logic of the pivot, the competitive moat of the NetNut network, the risks of operating in a consolidating proxy-market duopoly, and the plausibility of management's AI-infrastructure positioning narrative.

chapters.title: The Reinvention: How a Cybersecurity Pivot Became a Proxy-Network SaaS Company Hunting AI Training Data
chapters.body:
## A Company Remade

As of 23 May 2026, Alarum Technologies Ltd. occupied a peculiar position in the hierarchy of global software companies: too small for index funds, too profitable to dismiss, and too narratively compelling for the AI-era market to ignore entirely. Trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ALAR with a market capitalisation in the $50-60 million range, the Herzliya-based company had closed 2024 with $31.8 million in revenues, its first sustained net profit of $5.8 million, and a cash reserve of $25.0 million — a balance sheet that had roughly doubled in twelve months without a single equity raise. The stock, representing a thinly traded American Depositary Share structure where one ADS equals ten ordinary shares, nonetheless captured investor attention for a reason that had little to do with its current financials: management had planted a flag in the AI training-data market, and the flag had begun to look credible.

The strategic thesis Alarum's leadership had staked the company on was specific and falsifiable. Chief Executive Shachar Daniel, the co-founder who had guided the business since its 2013 inception, argued that the IP proxy network — a commodity-adjacent infrastructure layer for anonymous, high-volume web data retrieval — would become a critical-path input in the artificial intelligence supply chain. In Daniel's framing, just as cloud compute became a utility underpinning the prior decade of SaaS development, proxy infrastructure would become non-negotiable for every organisation building or maintaining large language models that required fresh, diverse, and legally defensible public-web training data. Alarum's NetNut platform, with its hybrid architecture combining ISP-direct node connections with a residential pool of approximately 85 million IP addresses, would provide durable differentiation against Bright Data and Oxylabs — the two better-capitalised private incumbents — by delivering higher success rates on contested sources at competitive bandwidth pricing.

Whether that thesis holds is what the thirteen chapters of this dossier examine. To understand the wager, one must first understand the company that made it.

## Three Phases, One Founder

Alarum's corporate history divides cleanly into three phases. In the first, from 2013 to 2019, Safe-T Group Ltd. — as the company was then known — built and listed a zero-trust cybersecurity platform targeting enterprise network-access control, listing on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange in 2016 and conducting a secondary Nasdaq listing in June 2018 under the ticker SFET. In the second phase, from 2019 to 2022, Safe-T executed a $9.7 million acquisition of NetNut Ltd. from DiViNetworks Ltd. — paid roughly 40 percent in equity and 60 percent in cash — and spent three years divesting the cybersecurity business, winding down a consumer-privacy VPN segment, and concentrating all commercial activity on NetNut's proxy-network platform. In the third phase, beginning January 12, 2023, when Safe-T formally rebranded as Alarum Technologies Ltd. and migrated its Nasdaq ticker to ALAR, the company has operated as a focused SaaS business: scaling infrastructure, expanding the IP pool, launching an AI Data Collector product line, and converting the first meaningful profits in its listed history.

## The Numbers That Define the Moment

| Metric | FY 2023 | FY 2024 | Q1 2024 | Q1 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total revenues (USD) | $26.5M | $31.8M | $8.4M | $7.1M |
| Web data collection revenues | ~$21.3M | $30.9M | — | — |
| Gross margin (IFRS) | ~69% | 75.1% | 78.5% | 67.5% |
| Net income / (loss) | ($5.6M) | $5.8M | — | — |
| Adjusted EBITDA | $5.2M | $9.4M | — | — |
| Cash and liquid investments | $10.9M | $25.0M | — | — |
| Net Revenue Retention | — | 1.27× (Dec '24) | — | 1.13× (Mar '25) |

The 2024 figures told a story of operational maturation: revenues grew 20 percent year-over-year, operating cash flow surged 93 percent to $8.9 million, and the cash position nearly doubled entirely through retained earnings. [Alarum Q4 and FY 2024 press release](https://alarum.io/alarum-technologies-announces-fourth-quarter-and-annual-2024-results/)

The first quarter of 2025 introduced a discordant note. Revenue fell 15 percent year-over-year to $7.1 million, gross margin compressed more than eleven percentage points to 67.5 percent, and net revenue retention — the metric management had cited as evidence of product-market fit — moderated from 1.27 to 1.13 in a single quarter. Management attributed the deceleration to demand softness within certain customer cohorts since mid-2024 and to infrastructure investment costs running ahead of anticipated revenue recovery. The company guided second-quarter 2025 revenues at $7.9 million, plus or minus three percent — a sequential improvement, but still meaningfully below the peak quarterly run-rate of $8.9 million recorded in Q2 2024. [Alarum Q1 2025 press release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001725332/000121390025081395/ea025370601ex99-1_alarum.htm)

The tension this creates is the organising question for what follows: 2024's profitability inflection and the AI-data-training narrative gave Alarum a credible growth story; Q1 2025's deceleration introduced legitimate doubt about whether that story is intact, cyclically interrupted, or structurally impaired.

## The Question the Dossier Must Answer

Can a micro-cap Israeli SaaS company — one with founder-controlled governance, thin ADS liquidity on Nasdaq, and an 85-million-IP proxy network built through a decade of incremental engineering — establish itself as critical infrastructure for the AI training-data economy? Or will Bright Data, Oxylabs, and the hyperscalers' own crawling capacity commoditise the proxy layer before Alarum's balance sheet can fund the scale required to compete? The chapters that follow assemble the evidence — financial, competitive, technological, legal, and geopolitical — needed to answer that question with precision.

chapters.title: Safe-T to Alarum: A Decade of Pivots, Divestitures, and the NetNut Bet
chapters.body:
## Herzliya, 2013: The Unit 8200 Shadow

The company that would eventually become Alarum Technologies was born in 2013 in Herzliya, Israel's coastal technology corridor north of Tel Aviv, in an entrepreneurial climate shaped as much by military service as by venture capital. Shachar Daniel and Amir Mizhar co-founded Safe-T Group Ltd. in a moment when the Israeli cybersecurity sector was producing startups at a rate that would define a generation of enterprise technology. The Israeli Defence Forces' signals intelligence unit, known as Unit 8200, had by then seeded dozens of companies across network security, encryption, and threat detection. Safe-T was not a Unit 8200 spinout in the formal sense, but it emerged from the same ecosystem of technically sophisticated founders who understood, viscerally, the problem of controlling access across untrusted networks.

The product concept Daniel and Mizhar pursued was zero-trust network access — the principle that no user or device should be implicitly trusted simply because it resided inside a corporate perimeter. Zero-trust was gaining theoretical traction in security circles in the early 2010s, but enterprise adoption remained nascent and the commercial category was crowded with larger incumbents. Safe-T built its offering around software-defined perimeter technology, targeting mid-market enterprises that needed to control remote access without the complexity of legacy VPN architectures. It was a technically credible idea in a market that would eventually prove enormous, but Safe-T was competing against players with far greater sales forces and balance sheets.

## From Tel Aviv to Nasdaq: The Capital Markets Journey, 2016–2018

Safe-T listed on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange in 2016, the conventional first step for Israeli technology companies seeking public capital. The TASE listing gave the company currency for acquisitions and a measure of institutional visibility, but the Israeli market's depth was limited for a software company of Safe-T's size. The logic for a Nasdaq dual-listing was straightforward: US institutional investors provided larger pools of capital, higher valuation multiples for software businesses, and the marketing imprimatur that a Nasdaq ticker conferred on Israeli companies seeking enterprise sales conversations in North America and Europe.

In June 2018, Safe-T completed that dual-listing under the ticker SFET. The timing was not auspicious — the broader technology market was entering a period of volatility, and SFET opened to limited fanfare. But the US listing accomplished its secondary objective: it positioned the company to execute acquisitions using Nasdaq-traded equity as consideration, a capability that would prove decisive within the year.

## The NetNut Acquisition: A $9.7 Million Bet That Rewrote the Company

The transaction that ultimately determined Alarum Technologies' identity was announced in April 2019, when Safe-T agreed to acquire NetNut Ltd. and related assets from DiViNetworks Ltd. for total consideration of approximately $9.7 million. The terms called for roughly 40 percent of the purchase price to be paid in Safe-T equity and 60 percent in cash — a structure that reflected both the acquirer's limited cash position and the liquidity the Nasdaq listing had provided.

DiViNetworks was a private Israeli network infrastructure company that had developed NetNut as a hybrid residential IP proxy network. The product's architecture combined direct connectivity agreements with internet service providers — a relatively rare and technically demanding approach — with a broader residential node pool, producing a network capable of routing web requests through millions of IP addresses in a manner that made automated traffic appear indistinguishable from organic user browsing. The business case for such infrastructure was well-established: e-commerce companies needed to monitor competitor pricing without triggering rate limits; brand-protection firms needed to detect counterfeit listings on global marketplaces; financial data vendors needed to scrape public sources at scale without being blocked. NetNut's IPPN platform addressed each of these demands.

To Safe-T's management, the acquisition logic had two components that were simultaneously contradictory and compelling. NetNut was, on its face, orthogonal to the zero-trust cybersecurity business: one product secured corporate networks against intrusion, the other helped customers anonymously access external networks at industrial scale. They shared engineering DNA in networking protocols but almost nothing else in terms of go-to-market, customer profile, or competitive dynamics. Yet the financial asymmetry was impossible to ignore. NetNut was growing at rates the legacy cybersecurity business could not approach, addressed a larger and more fragmented customer base, and operated on a SaaS consumption model that generated predictable, scalable revenue without the lengthy enterprise sales cycles that handicapped Safe-T's core product.

## Dual-Tracking and the Decision to Concentrate, 2020–2022

The three years following the NetNut acquisition were a period of institutional ambivalence that the company's filings document but management has rarely dwelt upon in investor communications. Safe-T operated both segments simultaneously, reporting cybersecurity and proxy revenues as separate lines, and for a period presented the combination as a coherent "data security and privacy" thesis. The framing was strained. The two businesses shared a balance sheet and a CEO; they shared little else.

The deceleration of the cybersecurity segment made the strategic choice easier than it might otherwise have been. Enterprise sales cycles lengthened, competitive pressure from larger vendors intensified, and the capital requirements for maintaining and expanding the zero-trust product roadmap grew inconsistent with the company's resource base. Management began a methodical divestiture of the enterprise cybersecurity contract portfolio during 2021 and 2022. Simultaneously, a consumer-facing privacy VPN product that Safe-T had built as a retail channel was wound down — the consumer VPN market had become brutally commoditised, dominated by scale players and prone to margin compression that made it structurally unattractive for a company of Safe-T's size.

By the end of 2022, NetNut was the company's singular commercial platform. The question was no longer which business to prioritise, but whether the corporate identity inherited from the cybersecurity era still served any useful purpose.

## Alarum: Etymology, Announcement, and the Question of Signal

On January 12, 2023, Safe-T Group Ltd. formally changed its name to Alarum Technologies Ltd. and migrated its Nasdaq ticker from SFET to ALAR. The company described the rename as a reflection of its completed transformation, choosing a word — *alarum* — that is a Middle English and Early Modern English variant of *alarm*, used historically to mean a call to arms or a rallying signal. The choice was deliberate in its archaic register: the company was positioning itself not as a cybersecurity alarm business but as something older and more urgent — a signal, an alert, a mechanism that puts systems into motion.

Whether the rebrand constituted substantive signal or cosmetic marketing is a question worth examining with some precision. The case for substantive signal is this: the change followed the completion of actual operational transformation. The cybersecurity business had been divested. The consumer privacy segment had been closed. The NetNut platform was generating the overwhelming majority of revenue. A new name aligned the legal and stock-market identity with the commercial reality, removed the confusion that arose when analysts and investors encountered a "cybersecurity" company selling proxy infrastructure, and gave the sales organisation a cleaner brand story for a market segment — web data collection and AI training data — where the Safe-T name carried no equity whatsoever.

The case for skepticism is narrower but worth noting: the rename did not change the company's technology, its competitive positioning, its customer base, or its financial trajectory. Those things had already changed. Alarum Technologies was effectively the same company it had been as Safe-T Group in late 2022; the new ticker was the final administrative act in a pivot that had been executed, largely, over the preceding thirty-six months. The name carried no inherent meaning to enterprise buyers and required explanation in every sales conversation.

## Validation and Its Limits: 2023–2024 and the Unresolved Epilogue

The years immediately following the rebrand produced the validation the pivot thesis required. Alarum reported ten consecutive quarters of year-over-year revenue growth through 2023 and into 2024. Web data collection revenues grew 45 percent in the full year 2024, reaching $30.9 million. Gross margins reached approximately 75 percent, reflecting the capital-light SaaS architecture of the IPPN platform. And for the first time in the company's listed history, Alarum achieved net profitability — a milestone that Shachar Daniel highlighted in investor communications as confirmation that the concentration on NetNut had been the correct strategic decision.

The growth drivers were discernible and, in retrospect, well-timed. E-commerce intelligence remained the core customer cohort, but a new category was accelerating: AI and large language model developers requiring large-scale, diverse, continuously refreshed web data for model training and fine-tuning. Alarum's management moved quickly to formalise this demand signal, launching an AI Data Collector product line in late 2024 that combined the proxy infrastructure with no-code scraping workflows and pre-structured datasets.

| Period | Web Data Revenue | Growth YoY | Net Retention Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY 2023 | ~$21.3 million | — | — |
| FY 2024 | $30.9 million | +45% | 1.27 (Dec 2024) |
| Q1 2025 | $7.1 million | –15% | 1.13 (Mar 2025) |

The unresolved epilogue arrived in Q1 2025, when revenues declined 15 percent year-over-year to $7.1 million, against $8.4 million in the comparable prior period. Management attributed the deceleration to demand softness from certain customer cohorts that had emerged in mid-2024 and to deliberate reinvestment in infrastructure and R&D. The net retention rate compression — from 1.27 to 1.13 in a single quarter — suggested that existing customers were expanding their spend more slowly than they had been twelve months earlier. Whether that compression reflected a temporary digestion period in the AI training data market or something more structural in Alarum's competitive position remained, as of the frozen snapshot date, unanswered.

The decade from Herzliya cybersecurity startup to Nasdaq-listed web data infrastructure provider had produced a company that was smaller, more focused, and more profitable than its predecessor — and facing a harder set of questions about growth, competition, and market definition than at any point since the NetNut acquisition itself.

chapters.title: The NetNut Stack: Hybrid Proxy Architecture, AI Data Collector, and the Website Unblocker Differentiator
chapters.body:
## The Hybrid Topology: Why Architecture Claims Matter

When Alarum Technologies acquired NetNut from DiViNetworks in April 2019 for $9.7 million, it was purchasing not merely a customer list but a specific engineering thesis: that the optimal proxy network is neither a pure residential pool nor a pure datacenter rack, but a deliberate hybrid of both. That architectural claim — and the degree to which it delivers measurably superior results versus single-topology competitors — remains the load-bearing pillar beneath every product line the company sells today.

The core of the NetNut infrastructure is a network of approximately 85 million IP addresses, organised across four node types: residential, datacenter, mobile, and ISP-direct. The last of these deserves particular attention. ISP proxies, also called Static Residential or Premium Dedicated Proxies in NetNut's commercial nomenclature, are IP addresses assigned by internet service providers to residential customers but hosted on datacenter-grade hardware — a hybrid node class that combines the low fraud-score profile of a genuine residential address with the latency and throughput consistency of a datacenter connection. This distinguishes them from peer-to-peer residential nodes, where the IP address belongs to an actual consumer device enrolled in a usage-sharing arrangement, and from traditional datacenter proxies, where the IP is registered to a commercial hosting provider and immediately recognisable as such by anti-bot systems.

The architectural logic of combining these tiers is straightforward: P2P residential nodes supply geographic and IP diversity at massive scale, enabling customers to simulate organic browsing patterns across millions of unique addresses; ISP-direct nodes supply session stability and fraud-score cleanliness for workloads where detection risk is high and speed is critical. Management has argued — in annual report disclosures and investor communications — that this hybrid topology yields higher request success rates than competing networks that rely predominantly on one tier, because target websites' bot-detection systems must contend simultaneously with traffic that looks residential in provenance and datacenter-grade in behaviour. Whether that claim holds across all workload categories is difficult to verify independently; the company has cited its 2024 PROXYWAY benchmark results as third-party corroboration, though PROXYWAY is a commercial testing service whose methodology reflects point-in-time conditions rather than continuous audited performance.

## Five Product Families, Five Customer Personas

NetNut's commercial catalogue comprises five distinct product families, each mapped to a different buyer profile and use-case envelope.

**Rotating Residential Proxies** are the volume workhorse of the portfolio. They assign customers a new IP address from the P2P residential pool on each request or at a configurable session interval, making automated traffic statistically indistinguishable from consumer browsing at scale. The customer persona is typically an e-commerce intelligence firm or price-monitoring platform that needs to retrieve millions of competitor product pages without triggering rate limits: the IP rotation ensures that no individual address accumulates enough requests to cross the detection threshold of even aggressive anti-scraping defences. Financial data vendors extracting public filings and market data at high frequency are a secondary cohort.

**Static Residential / ISP Proxies** serve customers for whom session continuity matters more than anonymity breadth. Account management automation — keeping a persistent authenticated session alive across hours or days — requires a fixed IP address that does not rotate mid-session and that carries the residential legitimacy to avoid account flags. Advertising-technology firms running ad-verification checks and brand-protection services monitoring social platforms for counterfeit listings are the characteristic buyers here, willing to pay a premium per gigabyte for the dedicated assignment.

**Datacenter Proxies** are the commodity tier: high bandwidth, low cost per gigabyte, no residential provenance. They serve workloads where target sources are not defended by advanced bot detection — bulk crawling of lightly protected sites, internal quality assurance, and load testing — and where the customer's primary constraint is throughput economics rather than evasion sophistication.

**The SERP API** abstracts the entire scraping problem for SEO and search analytics customers. Rather than requiring the buyer to manage rotating proxies, JavaScript rendering, and parsing logic for search-engine results pages, the SERP API returns clean, structured JSON — keyword rankings, featured snippets, local pack data — via a single authenticated endpoint. The customer persona is an SEO agency or keyword-rank-tracking platform whose core competency is analysis, not infrastructure; outsourcing the retrieval layer to NetNut is a build-versus-buy decision with an obvious answer for sub-enterprise buyers.

**Website Unblocker** is positioned as the apex product of the stack — relevant where all five of the above might individually fail.

## The Website Unblocker and the 100 Percent Promise

Alarum's management has characterised the Website Unblocker as an "AI-augmented anti-blocking service" with a claimed 100 percent success rate for data retrieval from target sources that deploy aggressive automated-traffic defences. Understanding what that claim means technically requires unbundling the four mechanisms the product integrates.

First, automatic IP rotation draws on the full hybrid network to substitute exit nodes dynamically upon detection signals or rate-limit responses, without requiring the customer to manage pool selection. Second, CAPTCHA solving — combining machine learning classifiers for image and audio challenges with human-in-the-loop fallback for high-confidence thresholds — resolves the most common access barrier encountered by automated clients. Third, JavaScript rendering via headless browser emulation allows the system to execute client-side code and retrieve dynamically populated content that a simple HTTP request would miss. Fourth, and most defensively significant, dynamic browser fingerprinting modifies the browser's reported characteristics — user-agent strings, TLS handshake parameters, font enumeration responses, WebGL renderer signatures — on a per-request basis, frustrating fingerprint-matching systems that would otherwise identify repeated visits from an otherwise rotating IP pool.

The 100 percent success rate claim is analytically most defensible as a conditional rather than an absolute statement: if a page exists and is publicly accessible to any browser, the Website Unblocker will retrieve it, because the cascade of mechanisms eventually produces a request that is indistinguishable from a legitimate human visit. The caveat, rarely foregrounded in marketing materials, is that success rate and throughput are in partial tension — achieving 100 percent often requires multiple retry cycles through different techniques, adding latency and compute cost. The November 2024 Fortune 200 enterprise win was cited by management as validation of the product's enterprise readiness: the undisclosed corporation reportedly conducted a large-scale competitive evaluation before adopting the Website Unblocker, implying that Alarum outperformed at least one or two named incumbent alternatives on success-rate metrics in that customer's specific use case.

The Website Unblocker is sold via managed API rather than self-serve configuration, with enterprise-tier pricing that reflects both the premium capability set and the customer success investment required to onboard large-scale deployments. This delivery model produces higher per-customer revenue concentration and longer sales cycles than the self-serve tiers, which partially explains why the Fortune 200 win represented a meaningful signal in investor communications.

## The AI Data Collector: Infrastructure Meets the LLM Supply Chain

The most strategically consequential product addition in the snapshot period was the AI Data Collector, launched in late 2024. The product represents NetNut's first deliberate step beyond raw proxy infrastructure into the data-as-a-product layer of the LLM supply chain.

In technical terms, "no-code AI-driven data collection" means that a customer without engineering resources can define a scraping target — a domain, a content type, a schema — and have the platform generate, execute, and maintain the extraction workflow automatically, using machine learning to adapt the collection logic when target pages change structure. The output is not raw HTML or unstructured text but pre-structured datasets formatted for direct ingestion into model training pipelines: cleaned, deduplicated, schema-normalised records with provenance metadata.

The commercial thesis is that LLM developers — particularly the mid-tier AI companies building domain-specific models rather than foundation models with proprietary crawl capacity — face a structural data procurement problem. Acquiring training data requires simultaneously solving web access (proxy infrastructure), anti-blocking (Website Unblocker), parsing (extraction logic), and quality assurance (deduplication and cleaning). Alarum is selling the assembled solution rather than the component parts, targeting a buyer who would previously have needed to integrate four separate vendor relationships.

The speed of revenue conversion has been striking: AI-oriented revenues grew from approximately four percent of the total in early 2024 to approximately 30 percent by the first quarter of 2025, though the denominator compressed as overall revenues decelerated. Management attributed the growth to both new AI-native customer acquisition and existing proxy customers expanding their consumption into the AI Data Collector tier.

## The NetNut Patent: Meaningful Moat or Marketing Asset?

In 2023–2024, NetNut was granted a United States patent covering core elements of its hybrid proxy network technology. The company highlighted the grant in investor communications as a competitive differentiator, and it does represent genuine IP formalisation of an architecture that management has developed over more than five years of production operation.

The analytical question is whether the patent constitutes a meaningful defensive barrier or primarily serves as a marketing signal. Proxy network technology operates at the intersection of networking protocols, software-defined routing, and browser automation — areas where prior art is extensive, open-source implementations are widely available, and the most sophisticated competitive tools are privately developed and proprietary rather than patent-encumbered. Bright Data and Oxylabs have their own substantial engineering organisations and are unlikely to be deterred from architectural innovation by a single patent from a significantly smaller competitor. The more plausible defensive utility of the patent is in deterring smaller resellers and white-label intermediaries who lack resources for patent litigation, and in providing investors with a tangible IP asset on the balance sheet. It is a real asset, but not a moat in the classic sense.

## Roadmap Signals from Management

On the Q4 2024 and Q1 2025 earnings calls, Shachar Daniel and chief financial officer Amir Mizhar signalled a product investment posture that prioritised AI Data Collector expansion, infrastructure densification, and enterprise go-to-market investment over near-term margin optimisation. Daniel described the AI data category as the company's "primary growth vector" for the next several years, framing proxy infrastructure as the platform on which data product revenue would compound. Mizhar indicated that Q1 2025 margin compression was partly deliberate — reflecting accelerated headcount additions in engineering and customer success — rather than purely demand-driven, a framing intended to contextualise the revenue deceleration as a trough in an investment cycle rather than a structural erosion.

The forthcoming product introductions implied in management commentary included expanded dataset catalogues within the AI Data Collector — pre-built, domain-specific training sets covering e-commerce, financial data, and public social content — and additional geographic node density to support enterprise customers requiring low-latency proxy egress from specific regulatory jurisdictions. Whether those investments translate to re-accelerating revenue growth in the second half of 2025 is the central near-term question for the investment case.

chapters.title: From Loss to Profit: Revenue Architecture, Margin Expansion, and the 2025 Inflection Test
chapters.body:
## The Numbers Behind the Reinvention

Three years of corporate restructuring culminated in a single financial statement. Alarum Technologies' [2024 full-year results](https://alarum.io/alarum-technologies-announces-fourth-quarter-and-annual-2024-results/), released in the spring of 2025, showed revenues of $31.8 million — up 20 percent year-over-year — alongside the company's first sustained net profit: $5.8 million in IFRS net income against a $5.6 million net loss the prior year. The swing was not cosmetic. Adjusted EBITDA reached $9.4 million, operating cash flow surged 93 percent to $8.9 million, and the cash balance on the balance sheet very nearly doubled. For a business that had spent the better part of a decade burning capital through an identity crisis, the numbers marked something genuinely new: a coherent, profitable, and cash-generative company with a single business to explain.

That clarity arrived just as a new complication emerged. By March 2025, the quarterly run-rate had stepped backward.

## Revenue Architecture: Five Years of Concentration

The structural story of Alarum's revenue base is one of progressive simplification. As recently as 2022, the company collected revenue from two materially distinct segments — the NetNut web data collection platform and a legacy consumer-privacy VPN service — alongside residual licensing from the divested Safe-T cybersecurity product lines. By 2024, the consumer segment had been reduced to a rounding error: $0.9 million out of $31.8 million in total revenue, representing a business being managed for wind-down rather than growth.

The table below reconstructs the revenue history through Q2 2025 guidance, drawing on [SEC EDGAR 6-K press releases and the 2024 20-F filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001725332/000121390025025287/ea0234101-20f_alarum.htm):

| Period | Total Revenue | Web Data Collection | Consumer / Other | YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY 2022 | ~$16M (est.) | ~$13M | ~$3M | — |
| FY 2023 | $26.5M | ~$21.3M | ~$5.2M | ~66% |
| FY 2024 | $31.8M | $30.9M | $0.9M | +20% |
| Q1 2024 | $8.4M | — | — | — |
| Q2 2024 | $8.9M | — | — | — |
| Q3 2024 | ~$7.2M | — | — | — |
| Q4 2024 | ~$7.4M | — | — | — |
| Q1 2025 | $7.1M | — | — | −15% |
| Q2 2025 (guidance) | $7.9M ±3% | — | — | ~−11% |

The 2023 step-up — from an estimated $16 million to $26.5 million — reflects the first full year of concentrated investment in the NetNut IP Proxy Network following the divestiture of the cybersecurity business lines. The [web data collection segment grew 45 percent](https://alarum.io/alarum-technologies-announces-fourth-quarter-and-annual-2024-results/) in 2024 to $30.9 million, driven by enterprise customer expansion, new product lines including the SERP API and Website Unblocker, and the early contribution from AI-oriented data contracts. This segment now constitutes 97 percent of group revenue — a concentration that simplifies the investment thesis while eliminating any diversification cushion.

The intra-year 2024 cadence is instructive. Revenue peaked at $8.9 million in the second quarter, then softened to approximately $7.2 million in the third quarter and $7.4 million in the fourth — a moderation that was already visible before the Q1 2025 miss and suggests the demand deceleration began in mid-2024, not at the start of 2025.

## Margin Expansion: From High-60s to 77 Percent

The gross margin trajectory over 2022 through 2024 is one of Alarum's most compelling financial arguments. The company entered the period with margins in the high-60 percent range — respectable for infrastructure-adjacent software but below what pure-play SaaS businesses typically command. By the [full year 2024](https://alarum.io/alarum-technologies-announces-fourth-quarter-and-annual-2024-results/), IFRS gross margin had expanded to 75.1 percent, with the non-IFRS measure — which strips out share-based compensation allocated to cost of revenues — reaching 77.0 percent. The expansion reflects classic operating leverage: the NetNut proxy infrastructure carries a largely fixed cost base (server co-location, bandwidth commitments, network maintenance), and incremental revenue drops through at high marginal rates once the infrastructure is provisioned.

The Q1 2025 gross margin of 67.5 percent therefore stands as the single most important number in the recent financial history — a regression of roughly ten percentage points from the prior-year comparable quarter's 78.5 percent. Management's stated explanation was front-loaded infrastructure investment: capacity was being added ahead of anticipated revenue recovery, compressing margins in the near term. The logic is credible in principle — proxy network operators must pre-provision capacity — but it has an uncomfortable symmetry with a revenue line that also declined in the same quarter. If new infrastructure were being installed for confirmed demand, the gross margin compression would typically coincide with or slightly precede a revenue acceleration; here both moved in the same unfavorable direction simultaneously.

The question of steady-state gross margin matters considerably for valuation. The business structure — primarily bandwidth consumption billed at a per-gigabyte or per-call rate against a partially fixed infrastructure cost base — suggests a natural range of 70 to 77 percent at scale, assuming volume grows into the provisioned capacity. At the lower end of that range, an EBITDA margin in the 20 to 25 percent range is achievable; at the higher end, margins approach the 30 percent achieved on a trailing basis in 2024 before the Q1 step-down.

## EBITDA Versus Net Income: The Adjustments Examined

Alarum presents both IFRS financial statements and non-IFRS adjusted metrics, consistent with Israeli technology company reporting conventions. The primary adjustments that bridge IFRS net income to adjusted EBITDA are share-based compensation expense — which represented meaningful dilution of reported earnings as the company granted equity incentives to its engineering and product teams — and depreciation of proxy network infrastructure assets, capitalised under IFRS and amortised over their useful lives.

The adjusted EBITDA progression underscores the profitability inflection:

| Year | IFRS Net Income / (Loss) | Adjusted EBITDA | Implied EBITDA Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | ~$(4-6)M (est.) | ~$2-3M (est.) | ~15-18% |
| 2023 | $(5.6)M | $5.2M | ~20% |
| 2024 | $5.8M | $9.4M | ~30% |

The gap between IFRS net income and adjusted EBITDA in 2023 — roughly $10.8 million — reflects the scale of non-cash charges that had historically obscured the underlying cash economics. By 2024, the IFRS measure had converged toward the adjusted figure, as the legacy restructuring charges and consumer-segment wind-down costs dissipated and the company's profitable trajectory became visible under both frameworks. Share-based compensation adjustments are standard across SaaS comparables, and Alarum's adjustment methodology does not depart materially from industry convention. There were no disclosed material one-time items in the 2024 results that would invite scrutiny of adjustment quality.

## Balance Sheet Transformation

The balance sheet at December 31, 2024 tells the story of the financial inflection as clearly as the income statement. [Cash and liquid investments reached $25.0 million](https://alarum.io/alarum-technologies-announces-fourth-quarter-and-annual-2024-results/), up from $10.9 million twelve months prior — a near-doubling that was achieved entirely through operating cash flow generation, not equity issuance. Shareholders' equity mirrored the move, rising from $13.2 million to $26.4 million. The company carries no material long-term debt.

[Operating cash flow of $8.9 million in 2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001725332/000121390025025287/ea0234101-20f_alarum.htm) — up 93 percent from the prior year — confirms that the adjusted EBITDA number is backed by cash rather than accounting construction. For a company with approximately $31.8 million in revenues, a free cash flow yield of roughly 28 percent is exceptional by almost any software industry benchmark. The capital intensity of the business is limited: infrastructure investments are reflected in operating leases and server co-location costs rather than large capital expenditure lines, and the working-capital cycle is favourable given the subscription and consumption-billing model.

The $25 million cash reserve, against a market capitalisation of approximately $50 to $60 million at the frozen snapshot date, implies that nearly half the equity market value is held in liquid assets — a characteristic more common among asset-heavy industrials than growth-stage technology companies, and one that provides meaningful downside protection while simultaneously reflecting investor scepticism about the forward growth trajectory.

## The Q1 2025 Inflection Test

The [first-quarter 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001725332/000121390025048496/ea024379701ex99-1_alarum.htm) introduced the central unresolved question. Revenue of $7.1 million was down 15 percent year-over-year, gross margin compressed to 67.5 percent, and net retention rate — one of the most forward-looking indicators in a consumption-based SaaS model — declined from 1.27 at December 2024 to 1.13 at March 2025. Q2 2025 guidance of $7.9 million, while a sequential recovery, implies an annualised run-rate of approximately $30 to $32 million, meaningfully below the growth trajectory that had prevailed through mid-2024.

Three interpretations compete. The first is cyclical softness: certain customer cohorts — particularly e-commerce and price-monitoring operators — may have reduced proxy consumption volumes in response to budget cycles or platform changes at the major marketplaces they scrape. This would be consistent with the moderate mid-2024 deceleration and would imply recovery as AI-oriented demand replaces the shortfall. The second is deliberate reinvestment: management's own framing, which positions the gross margin compression and revenue deceleration as the cost of provisioning infrastructure ahead of an anticipated demand recovery, particularly from AI training data customers. The third, and most concerning, is structural erosion: the NRR compression from 1.27 to 1.13 in a single quarter is not a trivial movement. Net retention rates at or approaching 1.0 indicate that existing customers are neither expanding nor churning in aggregate — the expansion cohort that drove the 2023 and early 2024 growth is no longer compounding. If pricing pressure from larger, better-capitalised competitors such as Bright Data is eroding average contract values, NRR could compress further.

Management's guidance that Q2 2025 would reach $7.9 million provides a partial test of the reinvestment thesis: if AI products, which reached approximately 30 percent of Q1 2025 revenues from four percent in the prior-year period, continue to ramp, the back half of 2025 should show sequential acceleration.

## Three Paths to 2026

A scenario framework helps calibrate the range of financial outcomes through end-2026.

| Scenario | Key Assumption | 2025E Revenue | 2026E Revenue | EBITDA Margin | Cash at end-2026 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Recovery** | NRR reaccelerates to 1.20+; AI products reach 40% of revenues; gross margin recovers to 74–76% | $30–32M | $36–40M | 25–28% | $35–40M |
| **Flat** | Revenues plateau at $28–32M annualised; NRR stabilises at 1.10–1.15; margins recover partially to 70–73% | $29–31M | $29–32M | 18–22% | $30–34M |
| **Deterioration** | NRR falls below 1.0; pricing pressure intensifies; gross margin remains sub-70%; AI ramp slower than guided | $26–28M | $22–26M | 10–14% | $24–27M |

In the recovery scenario, Alarum's $25 million cash position provides ample runway to fund infrastructure investment without dilution, and the AI data revenue line creates a credible path to re-accelerating growth — potentially justifying a re-rating from the current depressed 1.6 to 1.9 times trailing revenue. In the flat scenario, the business generates modest free cash flow and the balance sheet strengthens, but the growth narrative stalls and the stock remains range-bound. In the deterioration scenario, the company is still solvent — the cash cushion is substantial — but shareholder value erosion would be significant, and the strategic rationale for remaining an independent public company would come under scrutiny.

The Q2 2025 result, expected in the summer of 2025, will be the first meaningful data point to differentiate between these trajectories. If revenues recover to the guided $7.9 million and gross margin shows measurable recovery toward the 72 to 74 percent range, the reinvestment thesis gains credibility. If margins remain compressed and NRR continues its decline, the burden of proof will shift decisively onto management to explain why the 2024 inflection was sustainable rather than cyclical.

chapters.title: Quarter by Quarter: Management Commentary, Guidance Cadence, and the Narrative Arc of 2023-2025
chapters.body:
## A New Name, A New Narrative: 2023 Sets the Stage

When Safe-T Group Ltd. changed its Nasdaq ticker from SFET to ALAR on January 12, 2023, the rebranding was less a marketing exercise than a declaration of intent. Three years earlier the company had acquired a Tel Aviv proxy-infrastructure startup called NetNut for $9.7 million. By early 2023, cybersecurity was gone, the consumer VPN segment was winding down, and the entire commercial weight of the enterprise rested on a single product platform. Alarum Technologies was, functionally, a one-business company. The quarterly earnings cadence that would follow over the next two years would chart, quarter by quarter, just how well that bet was paying off — and then, abruptly, where it ran into resistance.

The full-year 2023 results — $26.5 million in revenue against a net loss of $5.6 million — told a story of a company that had cleaned up its balance sheet and its business mix but had not yet converted scale into profitability. Adjusted EBITDA of $5.2 million was positive but modest relative to the infrastructure costs the proxy network demanded. Gross margins in the high-60 percent range reflected the fixed-cost intensity of running a global server fleet before the operating leverage of higher revenue density could assert itself. Management described 2023 as a transition year, and that framing was accurate: the full-year web data collection segment grew meaningfully from the prior period, establishing the trajectory that would accelerate into 2024.

## Peak Velocity: Q1 and Q2 2024

The first quarter of 2024 arrived with $8.4 million in revenue — a figure that, at the time, represented the company's strongest quarterly performance and confirmed that the secular tailwinds management had been pointing investors toward were materialising in the top line. [Alarum Q4 2024 Results](https://alarum.io/alarum-technologies-announces-fourth-quarter-and-annual-2024-results/) Gross margins expanded to 78.5 percent, reflecting the operating leverage that management had projected: the infrastructure base was largely fixed, and incremental revenue was flowing through at high marginal conversion rates.

Q2 2024 proved to be the high-water mark. Revenue of $8.9 million represented 27 percent growth year-over-year and established a peak quarterly run-rate the company has not since recovered to. The full-year cadence — Q1 $8.4 million, Q2 $8.9 million, Q3 $7.2 million, Q4 $7.4 million — produced full-year 2024 revenues of $31.8 million, a 20 percent increase over 2023. [SEC 20-F Annual Filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001725332/000121390025025287/ea0234101-20f_alarum.htm)

| Quarter | Revenue | YoY Growth | Gross Margin | Adj. EBITDA (FY context) |
|---------|---------|------------|--------------|--------------------------|
| Q1 2024 | $8.4M | — | 78.5% | — |
| Q2 2024 | $8.9M | ~27% | — | — |
| Q3 2024 | $7.2M | — | — | — |
| Q4 2024 | $7.4M | — | — | — |
| **FY 2024** | **$31.8M** | **+20%** | **75.1%** | **$9.4M** |

The Q2 2024 record came against a backdrop of growing industry attention on AI training data. Proxy network infrastructure had historically been associated with e-commerce intelligence and ad verification, but by mid-2024 language model developers were emerging as a discrete and fast-spending customer cohort. Shachar Daniel, in investor communications through this period, consistently framed the AI training data opportunity as the company's long-duration growth engine — describing the proxy network as critical-path infrastructure for the teams assembling the datasets on which foundational models would be trained.

## The Q3 Correction and What It Signalled

The $7.2 million third-quarter print — a sequential decline of $1.7 million from the Q2 peak — prompted the first substantive test of management's narrative credibility. The step-down was not catastrophic in absolute terms, but it interrupted what had appeared to be a steady upward trajectory and raised questions about whether Q2 had represented a structural breakthrough or a cyclical high point. Q4 2024 recovered slightly to $7.4 million but did not approach the Q2 level.

Management attributed the second-half softness to demand volatility among certain customer cohorts, without specifying which verticals or whether it reflected competitive displacement, budget timing, or genuine consumption decline. The net retention rate of 1.27 recorded at December 2024 — meaning existing customers had, on average, expanded their spending by 27 percent over the trailing twelve months — offered some reassurance that the core customer base remained engaged. But the gap between the NRR signal and the sequential revenue deceleration suggested that new customer acquisition may have slowed, or that the cohort composition had shifted toward lower-volume buyers.

Full-year 2024 nonetheless represented Alarum's most important financial milestone since the NetNut acquisition: the first year of sustained net profitability, with net income of $5.8 million reversing a $5.6 million net loss in 2023. Operating cash flow surged 93 percent to $8.9 million. Cash and liquid investments at December 31, 2024 stood at $25.0 million, up from $10.9 million twelve months prior, achieved through operations rather than dilutive equity issuance. Shareholders' equity doubled to $26.4 million.

## The Fortune 200 Disclosure and the AI Repositioning

November 2024 produced what management regarded as a landmark validation event: the disclosure that an unnamed Fortune 200 corporation had formally adopted the Website Unblocker product following a competitive evaluation. The company did not name the customer — standard practice under enterprise NDAs — but the framing in investor communications was deliberate. Reaching a Fortune 200 account with the flagship anti-blocking product signalled that Alarum's technology could pass the procurement scrutiny of a large-cap corporation, a credibility threshold that smaller proxy vendors cannot easily claim.

Simultaneously, management disclosed that AI-oriented revenues had grown from approximately 4 percent of total revenue in early 2024 to roughly 30 percent of Q1 2025 revenues — a compositional shift that management cited as evidence of successful product repositioning toward the AI Data Collector launched in late 2024. The product combined proxy infrastructure with no-code scraping workflows and pre-structured datasets intended for LLM training pipelines, marketed explicitly to the same AI developers whose demand for web-scale data was accelerating.

## Q1 2025: The First YoY Decline and the Infrastructure Thesis

Against that constructive narrative, the Q1 2025 results landed with unusual force. Revenue of $7.1 million represented a 15 percent decline year-over-year — the company's first such contraction in at least ten consecutive quarters — and gross margins compressed sharply to 67.5 percent from 78.5 percent in the year-earlier period. [SEC 6-K Q1 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001725332/000121390025081395/ea025370601ex99-1_alarum.htm)

Management's explanation centred on deliberate infrastructure reinvestment. Shai Avnit, the chief financial officer, characterised the margin compression as front-loaded investment — server capacity, network expansion, and R&D — being absorbed ahead of anticipated revenue recovery rather than as a structural deterioration in unit economics. The Q2 2025 revenue guidance of $7.9 million, plus or minus three percent, implied sequential recovery without reclaiming the Q2 2024 peak.

The NRR compression told a more sobering story. The metric fell from 1.27 in December 2024 to 1.13 in March 2025 — a 14-point decline in a single quarter. That rate still implies net expansion within the existing customer base, but the velocity of compression is notable: if the trend continued at that pace for two further quarters, the company would be approaching flat NRR, which would mean existing customers were barely holding their spend, and all growth would need to come from new account acquisition.

## Guidance Methodology and IR Quality

Alarum's ±3 percent revenue guidance convention is a narrow-band disclosure that, in practice, functions as a point estimate with a thin confidence interval. Over the 2024 reporting cycle, actual quarterly results generally tracked within or slightly below the guided range, suggesting the model is neither systematically sandbagged nor aggressive. The Q1 2025 outcome tested that record: the 15 percent YoY decline appears to have been partially anticipated in how management framed the Q4 2024 earnings call, but the magnitude of the gross margin compression was not explicitly pre-signalled.

New customer disclosures in the Q1 2025 commentary — an Asian marketplace operator, a global electronics brand, and a European AI firm — were offered as evidence of pipeline momentum. But sell-side observers following the company have pressed on two questions that management has not answered with full precision: whether the AI revenue share figures are derived from new product SKUs or reclassified proxy consumption from existing customers, and what the payback period is on the infrastructure investment cycle that is suppressing near-term margins. Until those questions receive quantitative answers, the ±3 percent guidance precision masks a wider band of uncertainty about whether the second half of 2025 can return the company to the growth trajectory that the 2024 peak appeared to establish.

chapters.title: The Founding Duo: Shachar Daniel, Amir Mizhar, and a Board Built for a Micro-Cap Pivot Story
chapters.body:
## The Architects of Reinvention

Shachar Daniel has been the public face of every iteration of Alarum Technologies since before the company had that name. He co-founded Safe-T Group with Amir Mizhar in Herzliya, Israel, in 2013, drew on experience in enterprise technology and Israel's defence-adjacent cybersecurity ecosystem, and has occupied the chief executive chair continuously since June 2016 — across a Tel Aviv Stock Exchange listing, a Nasdaq dual-listing in 2018, the pivotal NetNut acquisition in 2019, the divestiture of the founding cybersecurity business, and the formal rebranding in January 2023. For a Nasdaq-listed micro-cap that has navigated three distinct strategic identities in a decade, that executive continuity is unusual and arguably stabilising. It is also, at times, the company's most significant governance constraint.

Daniel's public persona is that of a technology-ecosystem strategist who has identified a structural wave early and positioned a small platform to ride it. His language in investor communications is fluent in the frameworks of enterprise SaaS and AI infrastructure. In the first-quarter 2025 earnings release, he framed the revenue deceleration not as a demand signal but as an investment cycle: the company was, in his telling, absorbing short-term growth costs to build the infrastructure runway required for the AI data economy. The progression from proxy infrastructure toward AI-ready datasets — a market Daniel describes as a defining opportunity for the decade — has been the consistent through-line of his communication since at least mid-2024. How much of that narrative reflects genuine product-market clarity and how much is category opportunism is a judgment the board and investors must make repeatedly; the limited disclosure of Daniel's pre-2013 career trajectory in public SEC filings makes independent assessment of his domain expertise difficult. The Form 20-F filed in March 2025 contains a biographical section under Item 6, but detailed pre-Safe-T employment history is not prominently surfaced in press releases or LinkedIn excerpts available in the public record.

## Amir Mizhar: The Architecture of Dual Authority

The organisational design at Alarum reflects, more than anything else, the founding partnership. Amir Mizhar holds three concurrent titles: President, Director, and Chief Technology and Product Officer. In practice this means the individual who conceived and continues to shape the technical architecture of NetNut's hybrid proxy network — the 85-million-IP infrastructure, the ISP-direct connection model, the AI Data Collector product roadmap — also sits on the board and holds the second most senior operational title in the company.

That configuration is common in Israeli technology companies, where founding teams often retain dual operational and governance mandates long after listing, and where the distinction between founder-as-operator and founder-as-director is deliberately blurred. The structural logic is that Mizhar's technical authority is too central to the company's competitive differentiation to be separated from strategic decision-making. The NetNut product suite — from Rotating Residential Proxies through the Website Unblocker to the new AI Data Collector — is the product of architectural choices made and iterated by Mizhar over more than half a decade. Removing him from the board would reduce oversight independence; elevating a separate CTO without changing his title would create ambiguity. The current structure avoids both.

The resulting tension, however, is real. Mizhar's dual mandate as President and CTPO means that the board's ability to provide independent technical challenge to management's product roadmap is limited by the fact that the company's lead technologist sits on the board itself. The board cannot easily commission a credible independent technology assessment of, for example, whether the AI Data Collector represents genuine product-market fit or a marketing repositioning of existing proxy infrastructure, because the person who built that infrastructure is part of the board reviewing it. That limitation is structural rather than personal, and it is an artefact of the founder-concentration model.

## Shai Avnit: The Financial Translator

Shai Avnit, Chief Financial Officer, is the company's financial voice across earnings calls and SEC filings. His tenure predates the 2023 corporate rebranding, indicating he was recruited during the transition period rather than imported from an external finance function after the pivot was complete. Detailed biographical disclosures for Avnit — including appointment date, prior career, and academic background — are not prominently documented in press releases or investor relations materials; the Form 20-F Item 6 biographical section is the primary source for this information.

What is evident from his public record is his facility with the non-IFRS presentation that governs Alarum's investor communications. The company reports under IFRS as an Israeli foreign private issuer, but supplements those results with adjusted EBITDA metrics that exclude share-based compensation and other non-cash charges. Avnit is the primary explainer of the gap between IFRS net income and adjusted operating performance, and his quarterly guidance methodology — delivering revenue outlook ranges rather than point estimates — has been consistent through the growth and deceleration phases alike. Managing the NIS-versus-dollar cost structure is an ongoing operational task: a material share of the company's payroll, facility, and R&D costs are denominated in New Israeli Shekel, creating a natural FX headwind when the shekel strengthens against the dollar. How Avnit communicates that exposure, and whether the company uses financial instruments to hedge it, is relevant context for investors assessing earnings quality.

## The Board: Independence, Expertise, and Foreign-Issuer Carve-Outs

Chen Katz chairs the board, a position that places him as the nominal counterweight to the dual-founder executive structure. As an Israeli foreign private issuer, Alarum follows Israeli Companies Law governance rather than the full suite of Nasdaq's domestic-issuer requirements. Israeli Companies Law mandates the appointment of independent external directors and requires that the audit committee include those directors, but permits deviation from certain Nasdaq compensation-committee composition requirements that would apply to domestic U.S. issuers. The Form 20-F Item 6 sets out the complete board roster — including appointment dates, independence determinations, and committee memberships — but the prep data available for this chapter does not contain the full extracted roster beyond Katz's chairmanship.

What the governance structure makes clear is that the audit committee's independence is the floor requirement Alarum must meet, and the filing record suggests it does. Whether the board has adequate technology and AI domain expertise to provide meaningful challenge to management's product strategy is a separate and harder question. A board that governs a company whose competitive positioning now depends on claims about hybrid proxy architecture performance, AI training dataset quality, and the technical superiority of the Website Unblocker's CAPTCHA-solving stack needs directors who can assess those claims independently of management. The leadership data available suggests that governance depth on these technical dimensions should be scrutinised by investors reviewing the 20-F disclosures.

## Key-Man Risk: The Undisclosed Succession Problem

The Form 20-F risk factors section for Israeli technology companies typically flags key-person concentration, and Alarum's filing identifies dependence on senior management as a material risk — both co-founders are cited in the context of business continuity. No publicly disclosed succession plan exists for either Daniel or Mizhar.

The retention mechanisms on record are equity-based. Both founders hold options and restricted share grants under Israeli equity incentive plans, with vesting schedules tied to continued employment. The Form 20-F Item 7 major shareholders disclosure establishes the beneficial ownership positions above the five-percent reporting threshold, but the precise founder equity stakes and whether those positions have been reduced through recent open-market sales under Rule 144 or equivalent Israeli mechanisms require verification against the most recent 20-F filing. What is structural is that with no disclosed replacement bench at the VP or C-suite level, and no board-disclosed leadership succession framework, the departure of either founder would create an operational vacuum that would be difficult to fill quickly from the external market. The proxy network architecture, the customer relationships, and the AI product narrative are all, to a degree that is difficult to quantify externally, embedded in the founding duo's knowledge and relationships.

## Compensation Alignment: A Transparency Gap

As a foreign private issuer, Alarum files executive compensation in the 20-F rather than a DEF 14A proxy statement, which means the level of granularity typical of U.S. domestic-issuer disclosure — including the Summary Compensation Table structure required by SEC rules — does not apply. The 20-F compensation tables disclose aggregate remuneration for the executive group and for the highest-paid individual officer, but do not always provide the component breakdown — base salary, annual cash bonus, equity grant value — that would allow an outside analyst to assess whether incentive structures are calibrated to revenue recovery, sustained EBITDA growth, or AI-product penetration. That transparency gap is a feature of the FPI regime rather than a deliberate obscuring by the company, but it limits shareholder ability to evaluate whether management is being paid for delivering the strategic pivot or simply for tenure.

Taken together, the leadership architecture at Alarum Technologies is a founder-concentration story with the attendant virtues — strategic coherence, long-term commitment, and cultural continuity through multiple reinventions — and the attendant risks: succession opacity, structural limits on board independence, and compensation disclosure that provides less signal than domestic-issuer standards would require.

chapters.title: From E-Commerce Scrapers to LLM Data Pipelines: Alarum's Shifting Customer Composition
chapters.body:
When NetNut was folded into what would become Alarum Technologies in 2019, its customer base was largely indistinguishable from the proxy industry at large: price-comparison scrapers, SEO shops, and alternative-data vendors who needed large volumes of anonymised IP addresses to extract publicly available information at scale. By the first quarter of 2025, that profile had shifted materially, and not in the direction the company's earlier investor communications had emphasised. The fastest-growing cohort was no longer retail intelligence or even financial data — it was artificial intelligence, a vertical that barely registered in Alarum's revenues a year prior and by early 2025 accounted for roughly three in every ten dollars the company collected.

## The Established Segments

Alarum's customer base in the 2022-2024 period was anchored by five well-defined verticals that reflected the proxy industry's traditional commercial logic. **E-commerce and retail intelligence** firms — aggregators, price-monitoring platforms, and marketplace surveillance services — formed the historical core of NetNut's business. These customers required continuous extraction of product listings, inventory data, and pricing signals from geographically distributed retail sources, often across hundreds of thousands of SKUs per day, and valued the network's residential IP diversity because retailers' anti-bot systems were calibrated to detect datacenter-origin traffic.

**Advertising technology and brand protection** firms represented a second established cohort. These customers used proxy infrastructure to verify the geographic placement of digital advertisements, audit publisher compliance, and monitor brand mentions across domains in dozens of markets simultaneously — workloads that are structurally repetitive, high-volume, and geographically dispersed, which maps well onto a rotating residential proxy offering.

**Financial data and market research** providers constituted a third segment with a slightly different data-quality profile: these customers valued structured, reliable data extraction from financial-disclosure platforms, corporate websites, and economic databases, and were prepared to pay premium pricing for high success-rate retrieval. The SERP API product line served a fourth distinct cohort — **SEO and search-analytics agencies** whose workflows required structured search-engine result page data without the infrastructure overhead of managing anti-bot countermeasures directly.

A fifth segment, smaller in revenue contribution but meaningful for brand positioning, consisted of **corporate brand-protection and compliance** teams at large enterprises. The November 2024 Fortune 200 adoption of Website Unblocker was the most visible evidence of this category's potential scale.

Across all five legacy segments, revenue contribution was not individually disclosed in Alarum's public filings as of the frozen snapshot. The company reported web data collection revenues in aggregate — $30.9 million for full-year 2024, representing 45 percent year-over-year growth within the segment — and did not provide a vertical breakdown beyond the directional commentary that AI-oriented products grew from approximately four percent to thirty percent of revenues between 2024 and the first quarter of 2025.

## The AI Turn: From a Rounding Error to a Third of Revenue

The acceleration of the AI/LLM developer segment between 2024 and early 2025 was the single most discussed feature of Alarum's investor narrative during this period. Management described this cohort as comprising **large-scale AI model developers and LLM training pipeline operators** — unnamed, but characterised as "major global players" in investor communications — who required high-volume, clean, geographically diverse web data for training and fine-tuning foundational models.

The commercial logic of why proxy infrastructure became a preferred channel for these customers, rather than direct crawling by the hyperscalers themselves, rested on several structural factors. Large-scale web crawling from datacenter IP ranges triggers increasingly aggressive rate-limiting and blocking from source domains; the residential and ISP-origin IP pool that a service like NetNut provides mimics organic browser traffic at a scale that would be operationally complex and cost-prohibitive to replicate in-house. For AI training pipelines, where dataset diversity and coverage breadth matter as much as volume, a proxy network's geographic spread — across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific — delivered a distribution of source perspectives that a single-origin crawler could not replicate.

Alarum's late-2024 launch of the **AI Data Collector** product line formalised this relationship. Rather than selling only proxy bandwidth, the company packaged no-code scraping workflows and pre-structured, curated datasets specifically formatted for LLM ingestion — effectively moving one step up the value chain from raw infrastructure toward data-as-a-product. "AI-ready data" in this context meant content that had been extracted, cleaned, and structured in a form compatible with training pipeline ingestion formats, reducing the pre-processing burden on the AI developer.

The revenue trajectory implied by the shift from four percent to thirty percent AI contribution between 2024 and Q1 2025 was striking even against a declining absolute revenue base. If full-year 2024 web data collection revenues of $30.9 million included approximately four percent from AI-oriented products, that implies roughly $1.2 million in AI revenues for the year. If AI represented thirty percent of Q1 2025's $7.1 million total, that implies approximately $2.1 million in AI revenue in a single quarter — suggesting that while overall revenues contracted, the AI subsegment was growing at triple-digit rates on an annualised basis.

| Period | Total Revenue | AI-Oriented Share (Est.) | Implied AI Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full-year 2024 | $30.9M (web data) | ~4% | ~$1.2M |
| Q1 2025 | $7.1M | ~30% | ~$2.1M |

## The Fortune 200 Validation

In November 2024, Alarum disclosed that an unnamed Fortune 200 corporation had formally adopted the **Website Unblocker** solution following what the company described as a large-scale competitive evaluation. The disclosure was notable for what it confirmed as much as for what it withheld.

What it confirmed was that Alarum's highest-complexity, highest-price-point product — the AI-augmented anti-blocking service that combines IP rotation, CAPTCHA resolution, JavaScript rendering, and dynamic browser fingerprinting — had cleared the procurement and security review process of a company whose revenues placed it among the two hundred largest corporations in the United States. That evaluation process, typically multi-month for enterprise infrastructure decisions, implied that Website Unblocker had been stress-tested against competitors including Bright Data, the private-market incumbent with substantially larger IP inventory and a more established enterprise sales organisation. Management cited the win as evidence that the product's claimed 100 percent data-retrieval success rate was defensible under rigorous real-world conditions.

What it did not confirm was the identity of the customer, the contract value, the duration of the engagement, or whether the relationship had expanded beyond the initial Website Unblocker adoption into other product categories. Alarum's filings and investor communications offered no additional specificity on any of these dimensions as of the frozen snapshot date. The Fortune 200 reference remained a single data point — powerful for sales credibility, limited for financial modelling.

## Net Retention as a Customer Health Indicator

Alarum's net retention rate offered perhaps the sharpest observable proxy for customer-cohort health beneath the headline revenue line. The 1.27 reading at December 2024 — meaning existing customers had, on average, expanded their spending by twenty-seven percent over the preceding twelve months — was an exceptional NRR figure for a company of Alarum's scale, reflecting both the AI upsell cycle and the adoption of the Website Unblocker and SERP API products by customers who had previously used only the core proxy network.

The compression to 1.13 by March 2025 in a single quarter was correspondingly significant. The drivers of the decline were not individually quantified in management's commentary, but the available evidence pointed toward two distinct forces: **expansion pressure easing** as the initial AI upsell cycle matured, and **churn in legacy cohorts** — particularly e-commerce and SEO customers who had reduced consumption volumes in the demand softness that management had identified as beginning in mid-2024.

| Metric | December 2024 | March 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Net Revenue Retention Rate | 1.27 | 1.13 |
| Quarterly Revenue | ~$7.4M (Q4 2024 est.) | $7.1M |
| Gross Margin | ~75% | 67.5% |

Sustaining fifteen to twenty percent annual revenue growth from a base of approximately $29-32 million annualised run-rate required, at a minimum, that NRR remain comfortably above 1.0 from the existing customer base while new customer acquisition added incremental volume. A 1.13 NRR, while still indicating net expansion, provided a substantially thinner cushion than 1.27: it implied that legacy-cohort churn was absorbing a meaningful fraction of the upsell gains being generated by AI and enterprise customers. If the NRR were to compress further toward 1.0 — net-neutral retention — Alarum would be dependent entirely on new logo acquisition to sustain revenue growth, a fundamentally more expensive and uncertain growth model.

## Geographic Distribution and Regulatory Exposure

The Q1 2025 disclosures introduced three new named customer categories that provided the most granular geographic signal Alarum had offered regarding its customer distribution: **an Asian marketplace operator, a global electronics brand, and a European AI firm**. The disclosure illustrated both the geographic breadth of the company's commercial reach and the strategic coherence of the expansion: the Asian marketplace customer would plausibly require proxy infrastructure to monitor regionally fragmented e-commerce platforms across Southeast Asia, Japan, and China; the European AI firm represented demand-side validation of the AI Data Collector offering outside North America.

The proxy network's core value proposition was, by construction, geographically universal: the ability to retrieve public web data from any source, in any jurisdiction, through locally appearing IP addresses, was equally relevant to a Tokyo-based electronics brand monitoring competitor pricing on regional platforms as to a San Francisco LLM developer assembling a multilingual training corpus. The customer base's apparent global distribution therefore represented a structural advantage rather than a concentration risk in the traditional sense.

The more material geographic exposure ran in the opposite direction: Alarum's operational base was concentrated in Israel, with the Herzliya engineering hub housing the principal product development and infrastructure management teams. The company's 20-F risk factors noted shekel-denominated operating expenses creating a natural NIS/USD foreign-exchange exposure, and the broader geopolitical environment in Israel during 2023-2025 introduced a category of operational and reputational risk that purely US-domiciled competitors did not carry. Whether any enterprise procurement teams — particularly those in regulated industries or with US government adjacency — assessed the Israeli operational base as a concentration risk in their vendor evaluations was not disclosed, but the question shadowed the Fortune 200 win narrative as an implicit caveat in any assessment of Alarum's enterprise market potential.

chapters.title: David vs Two Goliaths: Alarum's IPPN Architecture Against Bright Data, Oxylabs, and the Private-Market Proxy Ecosystem
chapters.body:
## A Market Defined by Private Giants

The global residential proxy market is an unusual competitive arena: dominated by two private companies that collectively control the majority of enterprise contract value, yet measured primarily by the behaviour of the one public company small enough to leave a financial trail. Bright Data — founded in Israel as Luminati Networks before a 2021 rebrand — and Oxylabs, incorporated in Lithuania, have built what independent observers estimate are businesses generating $100 million-plus and $50–100 million in annual recurring revenues, respectively. Neither has chosen to list publicly. The consequence, as Alarum Technologies understood when it completed its own Nasdaq positioning in 2023, is that it occupies a structurally distinctive role: the only pure-play proxy-infrastructure equity accessible to public-market investors.

That distinction confers a narrative premium but not a competitive one.
