Bright Data operates a network reported to exceed 150 million residential IPs, maintains a broad suite extending from raw proxy bandwidth to structured datasets and a managed browser automation layer, and draws on years of enterprise relationships built during a period when Luminati Networks effectively invented the commercial residential proxy category. Oxylabs, though younger, has developed a comparable product depth — real-time web crawlers, SERP scrapers, and a data-as-a-service tier — and has reportedly pursued aggressive enterprise go-to-market spending funded by private capital unconstrained by quarterly earnings scrutiny. Against these two, Alarum's NetNut platform entered 2024 with approximately $31 million in annualised revenue and an 85-million-IP network — roughly half the scale of its largest competitor by IP count and a fraction of estimated ARR.

## Architecture as Differentiator: Examining the Hybrid IPPN Claim

NetNut's founding technical proposition, dating to its pre-acquisition origins at DiViNetworks, was a hybrid architecture that combined direct partnerships with internet service providers — specifically ISP-exit nodes — with a conventional residential IP pool sourced from consumer devices enrolled in the network. The ISP-direct layer, the company argues, delivers lower latency, higher throughput, and better success rates on targets that filter for datacenter or clearly residential traffic patterns, because ISP-exit IPs occupy an intermediate classification that evades common blocklists. Management has consistently positioned this as a structural advantage over pure residential networks: the IPs behave like residential assignments because they originate from ISP infrastructure, but they route through server-grade hardware that avoids the instability inherent in consumer-device nodes.

The 85-million-IP figure encompasses the full hybrid network — residential, static ISP, datacenter, and mobile nodes. Bright Data's reported network exceeds 150 million IPs across equivalent categories. Whether the ISP-direct layer constitutes durable differentiation is contested. The architecture is neither secret nor patented in its totality, though Alarum disclosed a United States patent grant covering core elements of the hybrid network in its 2023–2024 filings — a meaningful but partial IP barrier. Oxylabs has publicly described its own partnerships with ISP providers and dedicated datacenter infrastructure, suggesting that the hybrid approach has diffused across the top tier of the market. What Alarum retains is first-mover depth in the specific implementation and the institutional knowledge embedded in its ISP partnership agreements, which require bilateral commercial relationships rather than mere technical replication.

The Website Unblocker product — an AI-augmented anti-blocking service combining automatic IP rotation, CAPTCHA resolution, JavaScript rendering, and dynamic browser fingerprinting — carries management's most aggressive claim: a 100 percent success rate. That figure, disclosed in investor materials and reiterated on earnings calls, deserves contextual scrutiny. Success rate metrics in the proxy industry are typically defined relative to a specific set of tested targets, under controlled conditions, and at defined throughput levels; universal success rates across all target types and all traffic volumes are commercially implausible. The metric is better read as a marketing benchmark — "we resolve what others cannot" — than an engineering specification. Its commercial validation arrived in November 2024, when an undisclosed Fortune 200 corporation adopted the Website Unblocker following what management described as a large-scale competitive evaluation. That reference customer win, disclosed via a November 2024 press release, was the highest-profile enterprise validation in Alarum's history, suggesting the product at minimum outperformed alternatives in a structured procurement process.

## The Proxyway Benchmark: What 'Named Top Performer' Actually Means

The 2024 Proxyway Market Research report, an independent benchmarking publication widely cited within the proxy industry, evaluated residential and datacenter proxy networks across dimensions including success rates, speed, IP pool quality, and pricing. NetNut was named a top performer in the report. That classification carries real but limited weight. Proxyway's methodology is based on automated testing against a standardised set of target URLs — primarily e-commerce, SERP, and general retail sites — and the rankings are relative: the report typically segments providers into tiers rather than producing a linear ranking against which the precise gap between NetNut and Bright Data can be measured in absolute percentage terms. Bright Data and Oxylabs also receive favourable classifications in the same report cycle, meaning "top performer" is a shared tier, not a first-place designation. The value of the citation is that it provides independent corroboration, under non-Alarum test conditions, that NetNut's performance metrics are competitive with the market leaders — which, for a company one-fifth the size of Bright Data by estimated revenue, is a credible achievement.

## The Long Tail and the Hyperscaler Threat

Below Alarum on the competitive map, the proxy market fragments rapidly. Smartproxy — a subsidiary of the same Lithuanian holding group that owns Oxylabs — and IPRoyal operate at the middle market, competing aggressively on price and targeting developers and smaller businesses with self-serve, credit-card-accessible plans that undercut enterprise-tier pricing. Dozens of further proxy resellers — many sourcing IP inventory wholesale from larger networks, including potentially from the incumbents themselves — populate the long tail. This segment exerts continuous downward pressure on entry-level pricing, limiting Alarum's ability to compete in purely commoditised bandwidth markets without margin sacrifice.

The more structurally significant competitive threat comes from a different quadrant entirely. Google, Microsoft, Apify, and Diffbot each provide alternative data acquisition services that can substitute for proxy infrastructure in AI and ML data pipelines. Google's datasets, Microsoft's Azure data services, and Apify's actor-based scraping marketplace address overlapping use-cases — structured web data at scale — through mechanisms that do not require customers to manage proxy infrastructure directly. As LLM developers mature their data acquisition workflows, some portion may migrate from raw proxy bandwidth toward managed data-as-a-service offerings provided by hyperscalers with existing enterprise relationships, lower compliance risk, and scale advantages in storage and compute. Alarum's AI Data Collector product line — launched in late 2024, representing approximately 30 percent of Q1 2025 revenues against 4 percent in the prior-year comparable period — is a direct response to this threat: an attempt to move up the value chain from infrastructure provider to structured-dataset supplier, competing with Diffbot and Apify on ease-of-use and with the proxy incumbents on AI-workflow integration.

## Pricing Power and the Margins Question

Alarum's expansion of gross margins to 75.1 percent in 2024 — up from the high-60s range in prior years — has been cited by management as evidence of improving unit economics and infrastructure leverage. The interpretation is partially correct but incomplete. Infrastructure efficiency gains driven by server optimisation and IP-pool management can explain a portion of the margin improvement without necessarily implying pricing power in the traditional sense. The proxy bandwidth market has experienced persistent price compression at the commodity tier as IP inventory has scaled: per-gigabyte pricing has declined materially over the 2020–2024 period across the industry. Alarum's margin expansion is more plausibly the result of customer-mix improvement — a shift toward higher-value enterprise and AI-developer customers paying for premium products like Website Unblocker and SERP API, rather than raw residential bandwidth — than of broadened pricing leverage over the customer base. The Q1 2025 gross margin compression to 67.5 percent, driven by infrastructure investment costs being front-loaded, confirmed that the underlying margin profile is sensitive to investment cycles and not structurally protected.

## Competitive Position Scorecard

The following scorecard rates Alarum against Bright Data and Oxylabs across five dimensions. Ratings reflect the frozen snapshot as of May 2026 and are necessarily qualified by private-company opacity — the financial and operational data for both incumbents are estimates drawn from industry reporting, not audited disclosures.

| Dimension | Bright Data | Oxylabs | Alarum (NetNut) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Scale (IP network / revenue)** | ★★★★★ | ★★★★ | ★★★ |
| **Brand / enterprise recognition** | ★★★★★ | ★★★★ | ★★ |
| **Technology differentiation** | ★★★★ | ★★★★ | ★★★ |
| **Customer relationships (depth / NRR)** | ★★★★ | ★★★ | ★★★ |
| **Financial resources** | ★★★★ | ★★★ | ★★ |

Alarum's honest competitive position is that of a well-engineered third-tier player with a specific architectural credibility, a single patent, an independent performance validation, and one marquee enterprise reference customer. Its structural advantage is accidental as much as deliberate: the incumbent leaders chose to remain private, leaving Alarum as the default expression of public-market conviction in proxy infrastructure. Whether that is sufficient to compound shareholder value against two better-capitalised private competitors — or to survive the longer-run challenge from hyperscaler data services — is the question the remainder of this dossier examines in detail.

chapters.title: Timeline of Events: From the NetNut Acquisition to the Fortune 200 Win and the 2025 Growth Reset
chapters.body:
## April 2019: The Acquisition That Remade the Company

The corporate story of Alarum Technologies effectively begins not with its founding but with a single nine-page term sheet. In April 2019, Safe-T Group Ltd. — a Herzliya-based zero-trust cybersecurity startup that had listed on Nasdaq just eleven months earlier under the ticker SFET — agreed to acquire NetNut Ltd. and related assets from DiViNetworks Ltd. for $9.7 million, structured as roughly 40 percent equity and 60 percent cash. NetNut had built a hybrid residential IP proxy network capable of high-throughput, anonymous web data collection. The technology had nothing to do with network-access control or perimeter security; it belonged to an entirely different industry. That mismatch, in retrospect, was the point.

The transaction generated little noise at the time. Safe-T was a micro-cap with thin Nasdaq trading volume, and a sub-$10 million proxy-network bolt-on did not attract meaningful analyst coverage. The stock moved modestly on the announcement, then retraced. What the market did not price was the implicit strategic optionality: management had just acquired the only asset that would matter.

## 2020–2022: Shedding the Old Skin

The years that followed were defined by subtraction. Safe-T's cybersecurity product lines — the original zero-trust network-access platform — were progressively wound down and divested, as were the consumer-facing privacy VPN services the company had operated as a secondary revenue stream. Neither divestiture generated headline proceeds. The narrative was controlled liquidation rather than strategic sale, and the market largely ignored it. What the process did accomplish was a clean separation: by late 2022, NetNut was the company's only commercial engine, generating nearly all revenue and carrying virtually all growth momentum.

The proxy-infrastructure market had by then entered a multi-year expansion, driven by e-commerce aggregators, financial data vendors, and advertising-technology firms willing to pay recurring SaaS fees for reliable, large-scale access to public web data. NetNut's consumption-based pricing model — billing customers by data volume — captured revenue growth directly as enterprise data appetite expanded.

## January 2023: The Rebrand and the Signal It Sent

On January 12, 2023, Safe-T Group Ltd. formally changed its name to Alarum Technologies Ltd. and migrated its Nasdaq ticker from SFET to ALAR. The rebranding was more consequential than cosmetic. It removed the last branding residue of a cybersecurity identity that had become a liability in investor conversations and allowed management to present a coherent single-product narrative to institutional audiences. The [6-K filed with EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001725332&type=20-F&dateb=&owner=include&count=10) accompanying the name change marked the formal close of the transformation. The ALAR ticker attracted marginally improved trading volumes in subsequent months, though the stock remained firmly in micro-cap territory.

Around the same period, NetNut was granted a United States patent covering core elements of its hybrid proxy network architecture. The grant — combining ISP-direct connections with residential node partnerships — gave management a defensibility narrative to deploy in sales and investor materials, though independent verification of the patent's competitive moat remained difficult to assess. No material litigation deploying the patent had been disclosed by the frozen snapshot date.

## 2024: The Year the Thesis Paid Off

The financial evidence for the Safe-T-to-Alarum transformation crystallised in 2024. Full-year revenues reached [$31.8 million](https://alarum.io/alarum-technologies-announces-fourth-quarter-and-annual-2024-results/) — up 20 percent from $26.5 million in 2023 — with web data collection segment revenues of $30.9 million representing 45 percent year-over-year growth in the core business. More structurally significant: the company recorded its first sustained net profitability, with net income of $5.8 million reversing a $5.6 million net loss the prior year. Adjusted EBITDA reached $9.4 million. Cash and liquid investments, which had stood at $10.9 million at the end of 2023, effectively doubled to $25.0 million by December 31, 2024 — funded entirely by operating cash flow of $8.9 million, not equity issuance.

| Metric | 2023 | 2024 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total revenue | $26.5M | $31.8M | +20% |
| Web data collection revenue | $21.3M | $30.9M | +45% |
| Gross margin (IFRS) | ~69% | 75.1% | +610 bps |
| Net income / (loss) | ($5.6M) | $5.8M | inflection |
| Adjusted EBITDA | $5.2M | $9.4M | +81% |
| Cash & liquid investments | $10.9M | $25.0M | +129% |

Against this backdrop, two discrete events in late 2024 provided the highest-profile validation the company had achieved since the NetNut acquisition. In November 2024, Alarum disclosed that an unnamed Fortune 200 corporation had formally adopted its Website Unblocker following a large-scale competitive evaluation. The Website Unblocker — an AI-augmented anti-blocking service that combines automatic IP rotation, CAPTCHA resolution, and dynamic browser fingerprinting — had been the product management positioned most aggressively toward enterprise buyers, and the Fortune 200 win represented confirmation that the pitch had cleared a demanding procurement cycle. The stock responded materially to the announcement, though as a micro-cap with thin float, the move reflected a change in investor narrative as much as a change in fundamentals.

Separately, in Q4 2024, Alarum officially launched its AI Data Collector product line: no-code scraping workflows and pre-structured datasets targeted at LLM developers and AI training pipelines. AI-oriented revenues grew from approximately 4 percent of revenues in early 2024 to roughly 30 percent of Q1 2025 revenues — a trajectory steep enough to reframe the company's positioning in investor materials from "proxy infrastructure" to "AI data backbone."

## Q1 2025: The Growth Reset

The pivot from celebration to caution arrived with [Q1 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001725332/000121390025081395/ea025370601ex99-1_alarum.htm). Revenue declined 15 percent year-over-year to $7.1 million, from $8.4 million in the prior-year comparable. Gross margins compressed sharply, falling from 78.5 percent in Q1 2024 to 67.5 percent, as infrastructure investment costs ran ahead of revenues. The net retention rate moderated from 1.27 at December 2024 to 1.13 by March 2025. Management attributed the deceleration to demand softness in certain customer cohorts dating to mid-2024 and deliberate reinvestment in R&D and server capacity — an explanation consistent with the back-half 2024 quarterly revenue pattern ($7.2M in Q3, $7.4M in Q4) but not fully accounting for the magnitude of the year-over-year decline.

## Forward Catalysts and the Investor Watch-List

At the frozen snapshot date, four variables dominate the investment debate. First, Q2 2025 guidance of $7.9 million (plus or minus 3 percent) represents the immediate test of sequential recovery — beating guidance would confirm the Q1 trough narrative; a miss would raise questions about structural customer churn. Second, AI Data Collector penetration: management's stated ambition is for AI-oriented revenues to reach 40–50 percent of total, up from 30 percent in Q1 2025; achieving that target within 2025 would validate the product category and justify an expanded valuation multiple. Third, a second Fortune 500 or Fortune 200 customer disclosure would provide evidence that November 2024's win was repeatable rather than exceptional. Fourth, capital allocation: with $24–25 million of cash on the balance sheet — an amount approaching the company's entire market capitalisation in certain trading windows — investors are watching whether management will deploy it in M&A, share buybacks, or infrastructure, and whether any announcement arrives before the balance becomes a source of activist pressure.

## Regulatory Tail Risk and the Scraping Litigation Shadow

Web scraping litigation represents the category-level legal risk that proxy-infrastructure providers have not fully priced in publicly disclosed risk factors. The *hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn* saga — in which the Ninth Circuit twice affirmed that scraping publicly accessible data did not violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act before the case was ultimately settled in 2022 — established a partial safe harbour in US federal courts, but subsequent case law remains unsettled and the factual distinctions between permissible public-web crawling and impermissible access vary by circuit. Alarum's 20-F risk factors disclose the category risk; the company had not disclosed any active litigation or regulatory inquiry against itself as of the frozen snapshot. EU data protection authority enforcement actions against proxy providers operating in European markets represent a related but distinct exposure, given GDPR provisions governing the use of consumer-device IP addresses without explicit consent.

## The AI Premium and the Risk of Its Evaporation

Since late 2024, ALAR's market re-rating has been partly a function of AI-data-infrastructure enthusiasm rather than purely fundamental performance. If the pattern of hyperscalers developing proprietary web-crawl infrastructure accelerates — as Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have each signalled through investments in internal data procurement — the addressable market for third-party proxy services in AI training pipelines could compress faster than the current revenue trajectory implies. Equally, if inference-side efficiency gains erode the economics of retraining large foundational models, demand for incremental training data could plateau before Alarum's AI revenues reach the critical 40–50 percent threshold management is targeting. The AI-narrative premium built into the stock since November 2024 is, by that logic, a catalyst with a timer attached.

chapters.title: Patent, Proprietary Architecture, and the Trade-Secret Framework Behind the 85-Million-IP Network
chapters.body:
## A Two-Patent Portfolio on a Much Larger Operational Foundation

On 15 November 2023, Alarum Technologies announced that its wholly owned subsidiary NetNut Ltd. had been granted United States Patent No. 11,818,104, titled "Anonymous Proxying." The disclosure arrived less than a year after the corporate rebranding from Safe-T Group, and management was quick to frame it as evidence of durable technical differentiation. CEO Shachar Daniel called the grant an expansion of the company's intellectual-property portfolio that "strengthens our position in the market," while Moshe Kramer, vice-president of research and development, described it as motivation to "develop new technologies addressing evolving customer needs."

The patent is real and covers meaningful ground. The innovation at its core is what NetNut terms the "reflector" method: rather than routing all customer traffic through an intermediate proxy device — the conventional architecture, which creates throughput bottlenecks and latency — the system uses the intermediate node's IP address only to initiate the connection handshake with the target server. Subsequent data requests travel directly from the client to the destination, preserving IP-level anonymity without funnelling gigabytes of payload through a single choke point. The practical benefit is speed and scalability: the reflector model allows NetNut to serve high-volume enterprise customers without proportionally scaling centralised proxy infrastructure.

Alarum's patent filings also include US Patent No. 10,110,606, titled "Reverse Access Method for Securing Front-End Applications and Others" — a grant that traces its lineage to Safe-T Group's cybersecurity era and covers a dual-server architecture for securing network access without opening inbound firewall ports. That patent is listed on NetNut's intellectual-property page but is structurally a legacy cybersecurity asset; its relevance to the proxy and web data collection business is indirect at best, covering a network-access paradigm rather than proxy-network architecture. Taken together, the two patents constitute a modest but legitimate IP portfolio for a company of Alarum's scale.

## What the Patents Do Not Cover — and Why That Matters

The more revealing question is what the patents leave unprotected. US 11,818,104 covers a specific traffic-routing optimisation — a functional feature within a proxy session. It does not cover the hybrid network architecture that combines ISP-direct, static residential, and rotating residential nodes; it does not cover the algorithms that determine which IP address to route through for a given customer request, geography, or target domain; and it does not protect the commercial relationships with Internet service providers that furnish the static residential IP pool.

Those ISP relationships are, arguably, the single most defensible element of the NetNut platform. The ability to offer genuine ISP-assigned residential IP addresses — as distinct from VPN-masked datacenter addresses — depends on bilateral agreements with carriers who agree to advertise IP blocks on NetNut's behalf. Replicating an 85-million-IP hybrid network across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific requires years of partnership-building, technical integration, and ongoing commercial negotiation. None of that is patentable. It resides in contracts, operational muscle memory, and reputational standing within a narrow supplier ecosystem.

The same logic applies to the operational layer: managing tens of millions of concurrent IP identities, cycling addresses to evade rate-limiting, calibrating rotation frequency against success-rate metrics for hundreds of distinct target domains, and maintaining uptime across a geographically distributed server estate. These capabilities are, in the language of intellectual-property law, trade secrets — proprietary know-how protected by employment agreements, restricted access to technical documentation, and the practical difficulty of reverse-engineering a live network. They are not, however, statutory rights enforceable against a competitor that independently develops similar methods.

## R&D Investment: Scaling Up, But Below SaaS Norms

The financial profile of Alarum's research and development spending reflects a company transitioning from infrastructure operator to product company — but still prioritising network scale over software novelty. In fiscal year 2024, Alarum reported R&D expenditure of $4.5 million against total revenue of $31.8 million, representing 14.2 percent of the top line — up from $3.6 million, or 13.6 percent of revenue, in 2023. By the first quarter of 2025, quarterly R&D had reached $1.37 million on revenues of $7.1 million, implying an annualised intensity approaching 19 percent.

| Period | Revenue | R&D Expense | R&D as % Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY 2023 | $26.5M | $3.6M | 13.6% |
| FY 2024 | $31.8M | $4.5M | 14.2% |
| Q1 2025 | $7.1M | $1.37M | 19.3% |

For context, growth-stage SaaS businesses typically invest 20 to 25 percent of revenue in R&D; infrastructure-layer providers — companies whose value lies in network scale rather than application software — tend to land in the 12 to 18 percent range. Alarum's 2024 figure sits at the lower end of the infrastructure bracket, consistent with a company whose principal capital outlays have gone toward IP inventory expansion rather than software engineering. The Q1 2025 uptick aligns with Daniel's stated strategic intention:

> "We made a deliberate decision to increase investments in our infrastructure and products, aiming to meet the growing global demand for large-scale data solutions."

Whether the higher R&D intensity translates into defensible algorithmic capabilities — or primarily funds headcount growth maintaining the existing network — remains to be seen in subsequent filings.

## The AI Data Collector: LLM Integration or Open-Source Assembly?

The AI Data Collector, launched in late 2024, is marketed as a no-code scraping platform built on large language model technology. NetNut's product page describes a "large language learning mechanism" that decodes HTML elements from a target URL into scraping parameters automatically, with self-healing logic that adapts extraction rules when page layouts change and CAPTCHA-solving capabilities that, the company claims, "learn and evolve." The platform requires zero code from the customer and promises a 99 percent data-retrieval success rate.

Notably absent from any public technical documentation is disclosure of the underlying model or framework. NetNut publishes extensive developer guides comparing Playwright and Puppeteer as third-party tools that work *through* NetNut proxies — evidence that these open-source browser-automation libraries are treated as customer-side complements rather than embedded components. But the AI Data Collector's own architecture remains undisclosed: whether it wraps a commercial frontier model via API, deploys a fine-tuned open-source language model, or integrates a headless browser layer via Playwright or Puppeteer internally is not specified in any filing or product document reviewed as of the 23 May 2026 snapshot.

That opacity is itself informative. Companies with genuinely novel ML architectures typically highlight them in investor communications; the absence of such disclosure suggests the AI Data Collector is more likely a well-engineered integration of existing tools — LLM-guided element detection, industry-standard browser automation, and NetNut's own proxy backbone — than a foundationally novel AI system. The commercial moat in the product resides in the combination and the operational reliability, not in proprietary model weights.

## An Operational Moat, Honestly Assessed

The web scraping industry's tooling layer is structurally commoditised. Scrapy, Apify SDK, Crawlee, and Playwright are freely available, actively maintained, and capable of handling sophisticated anti-bot environments. Any developer with modest cloud budget can assemble a functional scraping pipeline; the constraint is not software but clean, scalable IP inventory. That asymmetry defines Alarum's competitive position with clarity: the company's defensibility is an operational and network-effects moat, not a patent-based or algorithmic one.

The 85-million-IP hybrid network, the ISP relationships sustaining the static residential pool, and the years of operational iteration that optimise success rates across target domains — these constitute the real barrier to entry. A new entrant could obtain US 11,818,104's reflector architecture through the published patent, but it cannot obtain NetNut's ISP contract portfolio or its institutional knowledge of anti-blocking countermeasures by reading a filing. That is, in the end, the honest answer to the IP defensibility question: Alarum's intellectual property worth protecting was never primarily the kind that gets registered.

chapters.title: Six Risks: Competitive Displacement, Revenue Concentration, Regulatory Exposure, Key-Man Dependency, Liquidity Constraints, and AI-Narrative Deflation
chapters.body:
## The Competitive Moat Problem

Alarum's most immediate structural threat is not regulatory or macroeconomic — it is the two companies that occupy the floors above it in the same building. [Bright Data](https://brightdata.com) (formerly Luminati Networks) and [Oxylabs](https://oxylabs.io) are private, Israeli-adjacent, and well-capitalised incumbents whose proxy pools dwarf Alarum's 85-million-IP network. Both have built enterprise sales organisations capable of penetrating Fortune 500 procurement cycles and offer product suites — residential, datacenter, mobile, SERP API, browser scraping — that map almost precisely onto Alarum's NetNut portfolio.

The risk is not that a competitor will invent something Alarum cannot match. The risk is a pricing decision. Should either Bright Data or Oxylabs elect to acquire Alarum's AI-developer customer cohort through aggressive volume discounts — a cohort that accounted for approximately 30 percent of first-quarter 2025 revenues against just 4 percent a year prior — the financial consequences would be severe. Alarum's infrastructure base is largely fixed: server co-location contracts, bandwidth commitments, and residential IP sourcing agreements do not scale down linearly with revenue. A 20-to-30 percent revenue reduction from the 2024 base of $31.8 million would cut roughly $6-9 million from the top line; against 2024's adjusted EBITDA of $9.4 million, that compression would push the company back toward breakeven or loss, erasing the profitability inflection that distinguished 2024 as the company's defining financial year. The Q1 2025 gross margin compression to 67.5 percent — from 78.5 percent in the year-ago period — demonstrates precisely this operating-leverage dynamic in reverse: costs are sticky, and revenue step-downs hurt disproportionately.

Alarum's sole durable competitive answer is its patented hybrid ISP-direct architecture and its claimed 100 percent success rate on the Website Unblocker product. The United States patent covering core elements of the NetNut network provides some legal moat, but the underlying technology is increasingly imitable, and Alarum's R&D budget cannot match that of either private competitor on an absolute basis.

## Revenue and Customer Concentration

Alarum's financial story is, structurally, a single-product company. In 2024, $30.9 million of the $31.8 million in total revenues — 97 percent — derived from the NetNut web data collection segment. The consumer privacy legacy earned the remainder in wind-down mode. There is no second segment to absorb a shock.

Within that single segment, the customer base carries its own concentration layer. The AI and large language model developer cohort is undisclosed by name but described by management as "major global players." This cohort's rapid rise to 30 percent of Q1 2025 revenues is simultaneously the most exciting data point in the company's recent history and the most dangerous dependency. LLM training budgets are determined by model development cycles and hyperscaler capital allocation decisions that are entirely outside Alarum's influence. If a capability plateau causes major AI labs to defer the next training run — or if a frontier model's training data requirements shift toward synthetic generation rather than web-crawled source material — Alarum's fastest-growing revenue cohort could decelerate sharply. The net revenue retention rate compression from 1.27 at December 2024 to 1.13 at March 2025, in a single quarter, suggests that existing-customer expansion is already moderating; the question management has not fully answered is how much of the Q1 2025 softness was attributable specifically to AI developer spend hesitation versus broader macro demand.

The Fortune 200 enterprise customer disclosed in November 2024 adds reference-account credibility but simultaneously introduces binary event risk: a single undisclosed account at enterprise-contract scale represents a meaningful revenue dependency whose renewal or non-renewal would be material to quarterly results.

## Regulatory and Legal Exposure

The legal environment surrounding automated web data collection has tightened materially since 2021, and Alarum occupies a category that draws regulatory attention from at least three jurisdictions simultaneously.

In the United States, the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act has been used by platforms including LinkedIn (HiQ Labs litigation) and others to pursue legal action against scraping operators and proxy resellers. The Ninth Circuit's 2022 ruling in *hiQ v. LinkedIn* offered some protections for publicly accessible data scraping, but the legal boundaries remain unsettled, and a company that sells proxy infrastructure specifically enabling commercial-scale automated data extraction faces ongoing litigation risk. Alarum's 20-F risk factor section — filed with the SEC in March 2025 — explicitly discloses legal and regulatory risks related to web scraping and data collection practices; specific disclosed proceedings, if any, would be material to investor assessment.

In the European Union, GDPR enforcement on automated data processing presents a distinct threat vector. Even where the source data is nominally public, the aggregation and commercial resale of profiles constructed from web-scraped data can trigger Article 5 proportionality and purpose-limitation scrutiny. Alarum's EU customer base — which includes the "European AI firm" cited as a new Q1 2025 enterprise partnership — transacts within this regulatory perimeter.

Israel's ISA disclosure requirements impose additional compliance obligations given Alarum's Tel Aviv Stock Exchange co-listing. Of the three jurisdictions, the United States poses the highest near-term risk: CFAA litigation is expensive even when ultimately unsuccessful, and a high-profile enforcement action or adverse ruling — even against a competitor — would create uncertainty that could cause enterprise procurement teams to pause or slow-walk proxy vendor renewals.

## Key-Man Dependency

Both founders are in the building, and the building is small. Shachar Daniel has served as CEO since June 2016, and his co-founder Amir Mizhar holds the combined President, Director, and Chief Technology and Product Officer roles — a title consolidation that reflects genuine dual-founder authority over both strategic direction and product architecture. There is no publicly disclosed succession plan. The 20-F's risk factor section is expected to identify key-man dependency as a disclosed risk, as is standard for founder-led micro-caps, but disclosure does not mitigate the operational reality.

Mizhar's particular importance is architectural: the hybrid ISP-direct proxy network that differentiates NetNut from commodity residential proxy resellers was built under his engineering leadership. His departure would create a product-roadmap vacuum at precisely the moment when the AI Data Collector product line — the company's highest-stakes growth bet — requires continued technical development and customer-facing credibility. The board, chaired by Chen Katz, operates under Israeli Companies Law governance; as a foreign private issuer, Alarum is exempt from certain Nasdaq independence requirements, and the resulting thin institutional oversight limits the board's demonstrated capacity to manage a CEO transition independently.

## Micro-Cap Liquidity Constraints

With approximately 69.1 million ordinary shares outstanding, structured as 6.9 million American Depositary Shares at a ten-to-one ratio, Alarum's Nasdaq float is thin by any institutional standard. At the frozen snapshot market capitalisation of approximately $50–60 million, a position of $5 million represents eight to ten percent of the total float — a scale that would trigger SEC reporting thresholds and create meaningful market-impact costs on entry and exit.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Ordinary shares outstanding | ~69.1 million |
| Nasdaq ADS outstanding | ~6.9 million |
| Market cap (frozen snapshot) | ~$50–60 million |
| EV / trailing revenue | ~1.5–2.0x |
| Cash & liquid investments (Dec 2024) | $25.0 million |

The thin float creates a compound problem: Alarum cannot effectively use equity as acquisition currency — any issuance at current multiples would be materially dilutive — and the share price is fragile on modest order flow. Prior to the 2024 profitability inflection, ALAR exhibited a market cap range of $50–120 million over a three-year window, driven by narrative shifts rather than fundamental re-ratings. The company's $25 million cash reserve as of December 2024 provides operational runway but does not solve the structural liquidity discount embedded in the stock.

## AI-Narrative Premium Deflation

The risk that closes the loop is perhaps the subtlest: the possibility that Alarum's valuation has been partially supported by investor enthusiasm for AI-data-infrastructure themes, and that this enthusiasm could degrade independently of the company's actual operating performance.

Alarum's management has been deliberate and disciplined in aligning its public narrative with the AI training data opportunity — "AI-oriented revenues" as a disclosed metric, the AI Data Collector product launch, and repeated earnings-call framing around LLM developer demand. This narrative positioning is legitimate; AI developers do represent a real and growing cohort. But narrative-premium compression is a real risk at the micro-cap tier, where the gap between a company's fundamental EV/Revenue multiple (currently 1.5–2.0x, already depressed relative to SaaS comparables at 4–8x) and a speculative AI-story premium can close quickly. If hyperscalers build proprietary web-crawling infrastructure at scale, if the AI model training market enters a visible consolidation phase, or if the broader technology sector re-rates AI-adjacent names, Alarum's market capitalisation could contract even if revenues stabilise at the Q2 2025 guided run-rate of approximately $7.9 million per quarter — roughly $32 million annualised. At that revenue level, a compression from 2.0x to 1.0x EV/Revenue would reduce the enterprise value by half, leaving a market cap that provides minimal cushion above the company's own net cash balance.

chapters.title: 2026-2030 Horizon: AI Data Backbone or Niche SaaS Survivor? Three Scenarios for Alarum's Strategic Destination
chapters.body:
## The Re-Rating Threshold

For Alarum Technologies to escape the 1.5–2.0x EV/Revenue multiple at which the market was pricing it at the frozen snapshot, management must produce evidence sufficient to reframe the company as genuine AI-data-infrastructure rather than a well-run but sub-scale proxy-bandwidth provider. The arithmetic of re-rating is blunt. At a market capitalisation of roughly $50–60 million in mid-2025, a move toward 4x–5x forward revenue — the lower end of the range at which investors price data-infrastructure businesses with durable growth — would require underwriting a revenue stream of $50 million or above, gross margins durably above 75 percent, a net retention rate sustainably north of 1.20, and a product mix in which AI-oriented workloads represent at least half of top-line contribution. Each of those thresholds is achievable from the current base; none is inevitable. What follows are three scenarios for how the next four years resolve.

---

## Scenario One — AI Backbone (Bull Case)

The bull case requires two conditions to hold simultaneously: that the structural demand for proxy-mediated web data in AI training pipelines grows faster than the supply of competing proxy networks, and that Alarum's hybrid ISP architecture proves defensible enough to command premium pricing from enterprise accounts. Neither is guaranteed, but both have partial supporting evidence as of early 2025.

On the demand side, the trajectory of AI-related revenues is striking. Management disclosed that AI-oriented products — principally the AI Data Collector and the Website Unblocker — had grown from approximately 4 percent of revenues in early 2024 to roughly 30 percent of first-quarter 2025 revenues of $7.1 million, an expansion measured across roughly four quarters that is difficult to dismiss as noise. The Fortune 200 corporate win disclosed in November 2024 added qualitative weight: a large-cap enterprise adopting a niche Israeli proxy provider's Website Unblocker after a competitive evaluation suggests both the product's technical credibility and the paucity of equivalently capable alternatives at that tier. [Source: Alarum 6-K, Q1 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001725332/000121390025081395/ea025370601ex99-1_alarum.htm)

In the bull scenario, that Fortune 200 win replicates across three to five comparably sized enterprises by end-2026. AI Data Collector reaches 50 percent of revenues by 2027 — implying a segment contribution of roughly $18–20 million against a total revenue base of $35–40 million. Annual revenue growth compounds at 20–25 percent through 2030, reaching $65–80 million by the end of the decade. Gross margins stabilise at 75–78 percent as the infrastructure investment cycle of early 2025 yields operating leverage. Net retention rate recovers to 1.20–1.27. The $25 million cash position — the largest the company had ever held at year-end 2024, up from $10.9 million twelve months prior — is deployed in a strategic acquisition of a smaller competing proxy provider or a scraping-technology company, adding network scale and customer overlap. At these metrics, a re-rating to 4x–5x revenue is defensible and implies a market capitalisation of $260–400 million, versus $50–60 million at the snapshot date.

The risk is timing. LLM developers are moving rapidly; Bright Data and Oxylabs are better-resourced incumbents with substantially larger proxy pools; and hyperscalers building proprietary web-crawl capacity could structurally shrink the addressable market for third-party proxy infrastructure in AI applications before Alarum has time to lock in multi-year enterprise agreements. [Source: Alarum Technologies 20-F 2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001725332/000121390025025287/ea0234101-20f_alarum.htm)

---

## Scenario Two — Steady-State SaaS (Base Case)

The base case assumes that the Q1 2025 deceleration proves transient rather than structural — consistent with management's framing of the demand softness as tied to specific customer cohorts and front-loaded infrastructure spend rather than systemic churn. Under this scenario, revenues recover from an annualised run-rate of approximately $29–30 million at the trough to $35–40 million by year-end 2026, supported by the Q2 2025 guidance of $7.9 million (implying sequential recovery) and the addition of the three new enterprise partnerships — an Asian marketplace operator, a global electronics brand, and a European AI firm — disclosed in the Q1 2025 earnings release.

| Metric | Q4 2024 | Q1 2025 | Base Case 2027E |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quarterly revenue | ~$7.4M | $7.1M | ~$10M+ |
| Gross margin | ~77% | 67.5% | ~72–75% |
| NRR | 1.27 | 1.13 | 1.10–1.15 |
| AI % of revenue | ~20% | ~30% | ~40% |
| Net income | Profitable | Compressed | $6–8M annual |

In this scenario, AI products grow to approximately 40 percent of the revenue mix by 2027 but do not achieve the 50 percent threshold that would trigger re-rating. Annual growth settles at 10–15 percent — respectable for a profitable micro-cap but insufficient to attract growth-oriented institutional capital. Pricing pressure from Bright Data prevents gross margin expansion meaningfully beyond 75 percent, and NRR stabilises in the 1.10–1.15 range, indicating healthy but not exceptional account expansion. The company remains comfortably profitable at $6–8 million net income annually, with the cash balance maintained or modestly grown. The stock trades in the 2x–3x EV/Revenue range — a modest premium to the trough multiple but well short of infrastructure re-rating. The $25 million cash cushion is deployed gradually in infrastructure reinvestment rather than acquisitions, and no material capital markets transaction is executed. This is a business that survives and improves incrementally; it is not a business that re-rates.

---

## Scenario Three — Niche Survivor and M&A Target (Bear Case)

The bear case turns on whether the NRR compression from 1.27 to 1.13 across the single quarter spanning December 2024 to March 2025 represented an early signal of structural customer loss rather than a lag in the expansion cycle. If Q1 2025's demand softness extended into the second and third quarters of 2025 — driven by AI developers consolidating purchasing on Bright Data's larger and better-integrated platform, or by the emergence of proprietary crawl capacity at hyperscalers — then the deceleration would prove cyclically intractable rather than transient.

Under this scenario, NRR falls below 1.0, signalling net churn for the first time in the company's SaaS history. Revenues plateau at $25–28 million with gross margins compressing toward 65–68 percent as infrastructure costs continue to be front-loaded against a stagnant top line. Adjusted EBITDA contracts sharply from the $9.4 million recorded in 2024. Management deploys the $25 million cash position defensively — extending infrastructure runway, funding modest R&D, avoiding dilutive equity raises — but does not execute a transformative acquisition. The AI Data Collector product fails to reach the pricing and NRR profile that would justify its positioning as a premium offering distinct from commodity proxy bandwidth.

In this environment, Alarum becomes a rational acquisition target for a larger data infrastructure player — a Bright Data, an Oxylabs, or a strategic acquirer in the enterprise data industry — at a modest premium to depressed market value. The company's attributes as an M&A target are real: a U.S.-listed legal vehicle with clean audited financials and IFRS-compliant reporting, a validated hybrid ISP proxy architecture protected by a U.S. patent, a profitable operating history, $25 million in balance-sheet cash, and an 85-million-IP network that would cost substantially more to build from scratch. A strategic buyer paying 2.5x–3.0x revenue on a $25–28 million base would acquire Alarum at $60–85 million — a modest outcome but a premium to a depressed standalone market price.

---

## Capital Allocation: The $25 Million Question

Whatever scenario materialises, the management team's deployment of the company's $25 million cash balance — the largest it has ever held — is the most consequential near-term decision. As of the frozen snapshot date, no formal capital allocation programme had been announced. The three logical uses are acquisition, buyback, and continued infrastructure reinvestment, and each carries a distinct strategic signal.

An acquisition of a competing proxy provider — even a modestly sized one with complementary geography or customer concentration in AI developer accounts — would accelerate network scale and NRR and send a clear message that management is in offensive rather than defensive mode. Given the micro-cap context, a $10–15 million cash acquisition is entirely feasible without dilutive equity issuance. A buyback programme, by contrast, signals management's view that the stock is undervalued on a cash-adjusted basis — at a $50–60 million market cap with $25 million in net cash, the enterprise value of the operating business was priced at approximately $25–35 million, or barely 1.0x the 2024 web data collection revenues of $30.9 million. That is, in principle, a cheap entry point if management believes the base case holds. Continued infrastructure reinvestment — the path of least resistance — preserves optionality but does not resolve the market's uncertainty about Alarum's strategic destination.

Management has not disclosed a preference in terms sufficient for investors to model against, making capital allocation the single most important earnings-call disclosure to watch in the quarters that follow the frozen snapshot. The answer will reveal whether Shachar Daniel sees his company as a buyer, a returner of capital, or a reinvestor — and that answer, more than any individual quarterly revenue print, will define which of the three scenarios above becomes Alarum's actual destination.

## Appendix E — Glossary

**ADS (American Depositary Share):** A Nasdaq-listed certificate representing an interest in a foreign company's ordinary shares; one ALAR ADS represents ten ordinary shares.

**Datacenter proxy:** An IP address hosted in a commercial data centre, offering high speed and low cost but more readily flagged by anti-bot systems than residential IPs.

**FPI (Foreign Private Issuer):** An SEC classification allowing non-US companies to file Form 20-F annually and Form 6-K for material interim disclosures, in lieu of 10-K/10-Q/DEF 14A.

**IPPN (IP Proxy Network):** Alarum's umbrella term for its hybrid network of approximately 85 million IP addresses enabling anonymous, high-volume web data collection.

**ISP proxy:** An IP address assigned by an internet service provider to a real subscriber but hosted on a server — combining residential authenticity with datacenter speed.

**NRR (Net Retention Rate):** Revenue from existing customers in a period divided by their revenue in the prior comparable period; an NRR above 1.0 indicates net expansion within the installed base.

**Residential proxy:** An IP address assigned to a physical consumer device by an ISP, appearing to target websites as ordinary household internet traffic.

**SERP API:** A managed endpoint delivering structured, parsed search-engine results page data, removing anti-scraping infrastructure burden from the end customer.

**Website Unblocker:** Alarum's AI-augmented data-retrieval service combining automatic IP rotation, CAPTCHA solving, JavaScript rendering, and browser-fingerprint spoofing; management claims a 100% data-retrieval success rate.

financials.key_finding:
Alarum Technologies achieved a significant financial inflection in 2024: full-year revenues of $31.8 million (plus 20 percent year-over-year, versus $26.5 million in 2023) were accompanied by the company's first sustained net profitability, with net income of $5.8 million reversing a $5.6 million net loss in 2023. The transformation was not merely top-line; adjusted EBITDA reached $9.4 million (from $5.2 million), gross margins expanded to 75.1 percent on an IFRS basis (and 77.0 percent non-IFRS), and operating cash flow surged 93 percent to $8.9 million. The cash and liquid investments balance at December 31, 2024 stood at $25.0 million, up from $10.9 million twelve months prior — a near-doubling that reflects both profitable operations and disciplined working-capital management rather than equity raises. Shareholders' equity similarly doubled to $26.4 million.

The company's revenue base is almost entirely concentrated in web data collection: $30.9 million of the $31.8 million 2024 total, representing 45 percent year-over-year growth in that segment, with a residual consumer-internet segment in terminal wind-down providing the remainder. This concentration is a double-edged characteristic — it means gross margin quality is high and the business model is coherent, but it also means the company has no diversification buffer if the proxy-infrastructure market faces demand or pricing headwinds.

The Q1 2025 revenue step-down to $7.1 million (minus 15 percent year-over-year from $8.4 million in Q1 2024) is the key unresolved variable in the financial story. Management guided Q2 2025 at $7.9 million plus or minus three percent — a sequential recovery but still below the peak quarterly run-rate of $8.9 million recorded in Q2 2024. Gross margins compressed to 67.5 percent in Q1 2025 (from 78.5 percent in Q1 2024), driven by infrastructure investment costs being front-loaded ahead of anticipated revenue recovery. With a market capitalisation in the $50-60 million range at the frozen snapshot date, ALAR trades at approximately 1.6-1.9x trailing twelve-month revenue — a depressed multiple relative to SaaS comparables, reflecting micro-cap illiquidity risk and growth uncertainty.
structural_observations: REVENUE BASE AND SEGMENT CONCENTRATION: Virtually all revenue (97 percent in 2024) derives from the NetNut web data collection segment, measured in USD and reflecting consumption-based proxy bandwidth and API call volume. The legacy consumer privacy segment generated diminishing revenue in 2022-2024 and has been substantially wound down, removing the consumer revenue contribution and improving overall margin quality. Full-year revenues grew from $26.5M (2023) to $31.8M (2024) to an annualised run-rate of approximately $29-32M based on Q1 2025 and Q2 2025 guidance, suggesting potential revenue plateauing after three years of 20-80 percent annual growth rates.

FISCAL YEAR CADENCE AND SEASONALITY: Alarum reports on a December 31 fiscal year-end and files as a foreign private issuer (FPI) using Form 20-F for annual reports and Form 6-K for interim disclosures. Quarterly earnings are released via 6-K press releases, typically 6-8 weeks after quarter-end. Based on 2024 data, revenue distribution was moderately back-half weighted: Q1 $8.4M, Q2 $8.9M, Q3 $7.2M (approximate), Q4 $7.4M, suggesting the mid-2024 demand softness that persisted into Q1 2025 was already visible in the second half of 2024.

MARGIN PROGRESSION AND QUALITY: Gross margin has expanded meaningfully over the 2022-2024 period — from the high-60s to 75.1 percent IFRS / 77.0 percent non-IFRS in 2024 — consistent with operating leverage on the fixed-cost proxy infrastructure base as revenue scaled. The Q1 2025 gross margin regression to 67.5 percent signals that the infrastructure investment cycle is absorbing cost ahead of revenue, a pattern that will need to reverse for the adjusted EBITDA margin to return to the 25-30 percent range achieved in 2024.

CAPITAL STRUCTURE AND BALANCE SHEET QUALITY: As of December 31, 2024, shareholders' equity was $26.4 million and cash plus liquid investments totalled $25.0 million, implying minimal net indebtedness. The company reports no material long-term debt in recent filings. The capital structure is equity-funded — Alarum has historically used Israeli shekel-denominated operating expenses (creating a natural NIS/USD FX exposure noted in its 20-F risk factors) but has not drawn on credit facilities in its recent operating history. With approximately 69.1 million ordinary shares outstanding (equivalent to 6.9 million American Depositary Shares, each ADS representing 10 ordinary shares), diluted share count for EPS purposes is modest.

DEBT VS EQUITY FUNDING HISTORY: The 2019 NetNut acquisition ($9.7 million, 40% equity / 60% cash) was the last significant capital deployment event. Since then the company has not executed further M&A, has not issued material new equity, and has self-funded infrastructure growth through operating cash flow. The $25M cash cushion as of end-2024 gives management the option to pursue either additional infrastructure investment, potential M&A, or a share buyback program — none of which had been formally announced as of the frozen snapshot date.

COMPARABLE PEERS AND VALUATION CONTEXT: Alarum's closest public comps are limited, as Bright Data and Oxylabs (the two largest proxy-infrastructure peers) remain private. The company trades closer to micro-cap software-infrastructure names. At the frozen snapshot market cap of approximately $50-60 million, ALAR's EV/Revenue multiple of 1.5-2.0x is a discount to both pure-play SaaS comps (typically 4-8x) and data-infrastructure companies (3-6x), likely reflecting micro-cap illiquidity, Israel-domicile geopolitical risk premia, and investor uncertainty about post-peak growth trajectory.

MARKET CAP VOLATILITY AND LIQUIDITY: ALAR has historically exhibited high share-price volatility consistent with its micro-cap status (~$50-120M market cap range over 2022-2025). The ADS structure (1 ADS = 10 ordinary shares, traded on Nasdaq) limits institutional ownership given the liquidity profile. Trading volume in the ADS is thin; major price movements have been catalysed by earnings surprises, the Fortune 200 customer disclosure in November 2024, and AI-narrative tailwinds in the proxy market broadly. Insider and institutional ownership concentration (per 20-F disclosures) may amplify volatility on news flow.

leadership.key_finding:
Alarum Technologies is led by its two co-founders, who have remained in executive roles throughout the company's listed life, providing unusual leadership continuity for a Nasdaq-listed micro-cap that executed a near-total business-model pivot. Shachar Daniel, CEO since June 2016 and co-founder since 2013, has been the public face of the transformation narrative — from cybersecurity to proxy infrastructure to AI data pipelines. His public statements across earnings calls and press releases are fluent in the language of AI-infrastructure opportunity, and he has successfully communicated the strategic rationale of successive divestitures to investors. However, detailed biographical disclosures in SEC filings (Form 20-F) are limited; Daniel's pre-2013 career trajectory is not prominently documented in public sources, making independent assessment of his domain expertise and prior track record difficult.

Amir Mizhar, co-founder and Chief Technology and Product Officer, holds the President and Director titles in addition to the technology leadership role, giving the founding duo dual control over strategy and execution. This founder-concentration model is common in Israeli tech companies and reduces agency risk but creates succession and key-man dependency.

Shai Avnit, Chief Financial Officer, is the primary spokesperson on financial matters in earnings calls.
